title: The Practical Life and the Soul as City
english: Commentaries on Ecclesiastes. 'Abundance of the earth is in everything, a king of the cultivated field is there' (Eccl 4:6). In the literal sense: no one is lord, master, or ruler of a field while it is being blamed for bearing 'thorns and thistles' (Eccl 2:6); but of a cultivated field, there is a king. He calls the king the owner. In the literal sense: if you see a cultivated field, know that it has a master and a king; just as if you see a chariot being driven in the manner of a charioteer, you realize you are receiving the impression of a charioteer; and if you see a ship being rowed and it must be steered in a certain way, you receive the impression of a pilot, even if you do not see him.

And those who occasionally introduce the idea that God's providence rules all things, say, if they are constructing [something], that it is providence; just as a fabric clearly shows that there is a weaver, even if the weaver does not appear, so one, seeing a cultivated field, receives the impression that it has a leader and a ruler. Furthermore: about whom then does he speak according to the literal sense? About the fields, saying regarding the king, the master, the owner, the one who cultivates: he names the king more appropriately. We sometimes call [God] lord and master. But it is also more powerful and more public to say so, if one sees a soul like a cultivated field, having been tilled, [with] offspring and wood and a multitude of offspring. For 'one carried a hundred, another sixty, another thirty' (Ps 126:2). When you see, therefore, a soul thus being farmed and having 'sown in tears' (Ps 126:5) and having itself ready for 'reaping in joy' (Ps 126:6), of this cultivated thing there is a king, a word meaning a leader, a word meaning one ruling and reigning.

But one should also take another analogy: the Church of God, according to the pious doctrines and the ethical works, and those who practice them, are called a field. When, therefore, one has according to the ecclesiastical canon and law and the mental dispositions and...

The practical life is a king for this field, because it has worked. But when you see false teachers and "churches committing adultery", know that this field has not worked truly; it does not have a king who praises it, but rather a tyrant or a robber. For robbers and tyrants especially pursue the wilderness.

And according to various thoughts, the soul is called sometimes a field and sometimes a city. And it is said concerning it: "The rivers of which the banks rejoice in the city of God" (Ps 46:4). And again: "You have been glorified, O city of God" (Ps 87:3). The soul, being thus disposed and having a straight canon of logic, is ready to receive [the Word].

Indeed, it is sometimes guarded by the world of the word and from those received through induction, but sometimes in a way other than how the following intends, let us take some starting point to depart from the history. "He who loves silver will not be filled with silver" (Eccl 5:10). As for the literal sense: the one desiring material things is never filled, but if it were possible for him to have all things under his own control, he would have loved this; therefore he is not insatiable of these things. It can be said concerning silver here: "it is not praised". For the one loving "the words of the Lord" will also be filled with "refined silver". For he does not always know "in part", nor, having transitioned from "out of the fullness", does he remain in the "from the fullness", but he will encounter eventually to approach "face to face" (1 Cor 13:12) the truth and to acquire the very "fullness" of the mind of Christ. Therefore, the discourse is concerning fake silver.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: True Goodness and Courage
english: little by little through observations

Having only those things, it is not possible to desire him and satisfy oneself a little; it is futile. For he is not able to consume all these things. It is darkness, and his effort is in vain and his desire has become empty.

In a multitude of goodness, those eating it were increased. Appropriately, we receive goodness as pleasure; for the good things are indifferent—some concerning the soul, some concerning the body, and some concerning external things. The things concerning the soul do not raise so much pleasure as toil and sweat toward beautiful things. For the things concerning the body and the external are full and productive of pleasure. If anyone does not have much pleasure raised by them, he has a 'multitude of goodness,' which is supposed to be goodness, since even those things on which he delights seem to be good, though they are not truly and principally good. Therefore, nothing is good that does not make the possessor good. Nothing good can be with sin, but with health and strength and beauty, sin can be. No one sins with a good, but with health we sin. Therefore, health is not a good. Thus the proposition was shown by syllogism.

Does the instruction mix with the word? That is, many strive for certain teachings and are greatly delighted by them, a 'pseudonymous knowledge.' They are increasing in the multitude of this pleasure. Those eating it seem to have something; the multitude takes in... and what courage is there from it? The good things are superior to the diminishing ones. For it is the beginning of seeing with his own eyes.

We say that true courage is a disposition prepared for bearing difficult things. For virtue and judgment are with it. For it is with prudence. For it has often been said that the virtues are held together. Certainly, the one having courage has also a theoretical reason; even if he endures some things and not others, he does not endure disgrace. And he is not puffed up by being entirely unrestrained or by exhausting the weaker ones; this is of presumption. An excess of courage has often been said to be rashness. There is, then, a certain courage, not a perfected courage. Thus, here we are not concerning true courage.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Body as Slave and the Soul's Resurrection
english: He says, but someone is held back by that which he thinks is courage. Rather, this person is merely reckless. We often take courage as being something attached to certain things: courage regarding struggles, regarding wars, courage regarding seafaring; and this kind of courage has no praise. It is a weakness. Even if someone becomes weak in body, yet bears things that come upon him with endurance and patience—this is an underlining of this: Job, who was weak and having been struck all over his body and having almost come to death, had the same courage of the soul.

"The beginning of life is bread and water and a garment and a house surrounding [one in] unseemliness." These things are the causes of living. And so such natural things are called the beginning of life. And here the name 'beginning' signifies the cause. Therefore, the cause of seeing is sight, the eyes. So he says this—so that I might also understand in agreement—he says this: let it be said, someone acts courageously by using the natural senses; he has the beginning of perceiving from the senses, but he does not keep these by his own courage. For many both courageous and strong men cast away their sight and were deprived of hearing and of the other senses.

Furthermore, regarding the ascent: "And what courage?" I do not say again that the courage which is virtue is "someone's"—though it might be said once that the prudence of Joseph was "someone's"—but regarding the vain courage, I say "courage" of "someone," not as something perfected. For the ascent, "the eyes are the beginning of seeing." I say that there are eyes of the soul which are enlightened, concerning which the apostle writes, "the eyes of your heart having been enlightened" (Eph 1:18). Concerning these it is said, "To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven" (Ps 121:1). Of these eyes is the beginning of seeing. If anyone does not have the "mind of Christ," he is not able to see rightly, if he has not been enlightened by the true Light.

Sweet is the sleep of the servant, whether he eats little or much; and to him who is filled, it is not possible to leave him to sleep. To sleep is taken from himself, but to eat and drink is taken from another. Even if little, therefore...

Eating, even in large amounts, happens because of the master's cause. Sleeping, however, is from its own nature. And since he sleeps without anxiety, having no care for possessions or the guarding of wealth, his sleep is sweet. But he who has much money does not enjoy even this. Furthermore, regarding the lifting up: 'sweet is the sleep of the slave.' We say this because the body is the slave of the soul. The body itself, as a body, has no care, or it has the appropriate sleep with rest. But the soul, when it has care for possessions, gathers much 'false knowledge'; those 'rejected' silver pieces destroy both wealth and sleep, the natural rest. For everyone's natural rest is called his own 'sleep' and slumber. Behold, he indeed says: 'Behold the reward,' he says, of the 'worker' who has become ungrateful, if he sleeps in the house of the owner, it accuses him. Not that the silver sleeps; he has said that staying in the house is his 'sleep.' The body therefore has the natural rest—I do not say the unrestrained, nor the insatiable desire for food, but the appropriate one.

This is to be understood: the things called morally good... since again they do not think about the soul as being the underlying reality. And some think that the allegories, of which Apollinaris is one, are mere re-paintings of those things happening sensuously. If one hears that 'a young lamb was raised up,' having cast away this very thing, the impious one has descended to ultimate death. The Savior, therefore, if he turns someone away from sin and impiety, has worked a resurrection. He who knows the soul—I say paradoxically, as an opponent currently thinking—knowing the magnitude of the soul and its salvation, sets nothing against the body, to restore a man to sight and to walk without hindrance from lameness. For the daughter of the chief synagogue, having been justified, 'has not died' (Luke 18:43). Again, those rising for the sake of the soul have it forever. Those things are vain, as regards a certain logic—not simply vain, but as regards the superiority of the greater things, just as the 'vanity of vanities' (Ecclesiastes 1:2) was given, that the temporary creations of God possess much beauty. Indeed, to him...

title: The Slavery of Wealth and the Sickness of Care
english: In the body, one will see its harmonies, for it is impossible for anyone to do anything except God. However, regarding the invisible and the things above, it is vanity (Eccl 1:2). Therefore, the soul has not been subjected to it.

He says that in time, in a certain way, he is a slave, obedient and private in his knowledge—and he is rich, having gathered many observations—and the sleep of one who thinks himself a slave and a slave-servant is sweet, whether he perceives little or much. And if he has the practice, so that this slave may have the 'spirit' of 'slavery,' he is not yet a 'son.' He is subject to the fear of judgment and 'abstains' from evil—if it must be said that he abstains—from the 'fear of punishment.' This, then, is a slave moved by the fear of the law.

Another, thinking to be in many [things], but having erred, has the care that does not permit him to sleep, a vain care. There is a sickness, which I saw under the sun (Eccl 2:18), a wealth guarded by one for his own wickedness, and that wealth will be lost in evil distraction. He says such things: For what is the purpose of someone's wealth? It is evident that even there the master of wealth is the wealth itself. This, then, is the one who has a sweetness from someone, and he himself is the master of the wealth; just as he is able to use the wealth well, holding it and not serving it, that is, the mammon (Matt 6:24), in this way wealth can hold the possessor; and woe to him, when he becomes a lover of silver, when he becomes a slave to mammon. He says, therefore, that such is 'wealth guarded by it.' He did not say simply the wealth itself, but 'guarded by it.' This is the wealth of the possessor. Thus also: how all painful things are endured for the sake of his acquisition.

And the terror of the sickness is this: neither he himself enjoys it, nor does any of his successors. Furthermore, is it not 'that wealth will be lost in evil distraction'? There is wealth being lost by suddenness or by being snatched away by wars or robbers having become strong and finding and taking it. This is not being taken in distraction. But when someone becomes a sailor or does other things for the sake of mobile wealth to gain much, often he is lost in the distraction. And we say to be distracted is to have [thoughts] about...
a deceptive snare

title: The Rich Fool and the Nature of His Loss
english: in grief and anger

Here, having [wealth] in opposition to what his father had—the one who gathered wealth through toil—and his mother, who bequeathed him a possession. He will turn back to go as he has come, and he will take nothing of his toil. The fact of the history is clear: he takes nothing of what he labored for. He lets them go and did not know at the time, even if they come upon his enemies. 'He stores up,' he says, 'and does not know for whom he gathers them' (Luke 12:20). And the matter of the upward leading has been said already, that he does not take away anything of what his father and his mother, according to wickedness, make wealthy. Therefore, a praiseworthy mother may also be taken; here she has come to godliness, so that she may possess... [text illegible] ...to enjoy... and indeed this is an evil sickness; for just as it came to be, so it will depart. — Thus it is necessary to take [meaning]: if the entering into a place signifies a local entrance, so also the exiting. For I do not say that the one who entered into this city went out from wickedness, but rather he entered here from another land or city. And what is his abundance, for which he toils toward the wind? His toil becomes wind, that is, his wealth is being overturned by nature; it is not becoming his own, not being held, so as even to be sent to a son. And indeed all his days are in darkness and in mourning. Darkness here means ignorance and the lack of clarity of things. And he mourns, missing those things which he hoped for, from which he thinks he has a pleasant life. And something stands before him. For mourning is raised up over death. In a certain way, therefore, he has died while living, 'and all his days are in darkness and he mourns' (Luke 12:21). 'And the one who squanders,' he says, 'has died while living' (Luke 12:20). If he has died, he is not worthy of being mourned; it is not necessary to raise up mourning over her. For indeed the empty lives living, but he has died, having cast away the life of salvation, the blessed life, as if he had not squandered [it] living according to the human [way].

title: The distinction between temporal and spiritual longevity
english: Her life. Even this... [lacuna] ...and drinking. From which he labored, etc. is. Regarding the ascent: 'Behold, I saw good, it is beautiful.' This good is useful and at the same time praiseworthy; for it was calling itself both good and beautiful. It is indeed praiseworthy to be called beautiful, but the useful and choice thing is good. If anyone eats the bread of life from the fruit of the 'tree of life' (Gen 2:9) and the flesh of Jesus, he shows good and beautiful to his soul, but I say to the one receiving it, [it is] good. And the striving to have good is [itself] good. For not everyone who is benefited is praised by men. Indeed, many of the flesh-lovers neither praise nor accept being medically cut or burned. It is good, but it does not become beautiful to the one receiving benefit from these things. For not everything good is beautiful and choice. It is said, 'to the...' [lacuna] ...they say it is beautiful, but it is not indeed good. For it is not possible to improve it.

Regarding the ascent: 'In his labor, by which he labors under the sun' (Eccl 1:3). He labors, toiling and wearying himself for the sake of the acquisition of virtue and divine knowledge. And because of sinning, some wise men are sometimes lost... [lacuna] ...simply and nothing... [lacuna] ...him. If, therefore, he eats and drinks such a thing, he labors. And according to the same ascent, it happens through the deficiency of food and drink—if, indeed, his soul thus eats and thirsts for goodness. For those who handle virtue well and wish to be called wise, they eat and drink not for the sake of the beautiful, but because they wish to be considered such; they read and attend to the readings, but they do not show good to their souls. For they do not handle it because it is good, but because it brings them praise; it is not good if they do not possess virtue as it ought to be possessed. They eat and drink to be distracted. [They consume] a number of the days of his life, which God gave to him, because it is part of Him. This he says regarding the explicit [text]: 'The time of men's life has been measured out by providence' (Job 14:5); and some live many years...

Regarding 'the few': for it is blessed the one who has possessed wealth—to those I speak—to enjoy it in the greatest number of years in which he lives in this life; that is, it is chance for him to be able to 'eat and drink' [Ps 104:5], to enjoy the 'number of the days of his life'. It was not for himself long-lasting or short-lasting, but it is judged by God how many years are allotted to each. This therefore is 'part of it', to enjoy the pleasant things through life, for which one toils and labors.

According to history, this is so. According to anagogical sense, this says, that if someone labors for the acquisition of truly good things and possesses them remaining through all the life of himself, it will be for his good. For he will be transferred from virtue to another place, to another region. When in the Scripture there is laid down a life praised or reproached with long duration, we do not take these things according to this immediate time measured by the sun, but rather 'the righteous', he says, 'will make much in wealth many years'. And again: 'the years of the ungodly will be shortened'. This does not appear according to history.

Thus indeed we take them: if 'the righteous' are rich, 'making much in wealth many years', this wealth of theirs is light. And the light measures out to them 'years'—years not these measured from the sensible sun, but by the 'sun of righteousness'. Thus indeed he says regarding 'the one honoring the father and the mother' [Ex 20:12] to fare well, because he is 'long-lived' or many-dayed. And this is not found undivided according to history. Many indeed, honoring parents, departed life prematurely.

The 'righteous' who happen according to the Gospel to be 'making much in wealth many years', while the years of the ungodly, even if they have a long-duration life here, 'are shortened'. I say: someone has wealth in false meanings; light will not remain to him after these things; therefore the years of the one thus illuminated were shortened; for until the present life he enjoys the seeming illumination; but the 'righteous' have the illumination even after these things. For 'the righteous will shine like the sun' [Matt 13:43]. He calls the 'sun' the 'sun of righteousness'. And indeed every man, to whom God gave wealth and existing and...

title: Proportional Distribution of Spiritual Gifts
english: The power to eat from it, to take a part of it, and to be glad in its labor—this is a gift of God. Wealth was given to a man so that he might eat and be glad from it, and therefore this gift was from God.

Often one uses the gift and enjoys what is in it, but sometimes one fails to do so, either because he himself, through much stinginess, consumes nothing toward being glad, or because he is hindered by sickness or some other circumstance. This stated thing is this: if anyone receives money so that he may be useful, and this is to be a gift of God. And He gives according to the needs of those asking.

Furthermore, what is 'in labor'? We have said 'from labor.' Furthermore, if it was a gift of God? I was saying what even the apostle says: 'that I often intended to come to you' (1 Cor 4:15). For what reason then? 'That I might impart to you a spiritual gift' (1 Cor 12:9). And I was saying that not all things given by God are spiritual gifts. Whenever anyone receives a 'word of wisdom,' a 'word of knowledge,' and some other virtue, he has received a spiritual grace; but not if someone receives wealth or health or something of that kind; he has received a gift of God and a grace, but not a spiritual one.

The Lord 'causes death and makes alive' (1 Sam 2:6). If He 'makes alive,' [meaning] grain, wine, this very life, He has provided, but not a spiritual gift. The Lord 'appoints kings and removes them' (Dan 2:21). The authorities given to the rulers are certainly not 'spiritual gifts.' And the grace here, which is the gift, is not spiritual, being sensible and human.

Furthermore, the ascent: 'and indeed every man to whom God gave' (Acts 20:35). I still have the end of the statement. If he has much money, if he has myriads of grain and much wine, he is not able to eat or drink everything, but he has a gift; which he is able to receive, the sufficient food, even until being satisfied, and that similarly, 'this is a gift of God.' If, therefore, anyone eats or drinks beyond what is necessary, he does not have these things as a gift of God, but as gifts of pleasure.

And toward the ascent, thus: God gives wisdom and the 'wealth' in wisdom. And the 'existing things,' the contemplations of wisdom, so that the man might eat and drink from which he received, the bread of wisdom.

so that its 'water' might be the 'wine' which he turned into a basin. And 'this' indeed is the 'house of God'. If one receives the spiritual thing as it ought, this gift is moreover a 'part of it'. You know that the parts are primarily given according to a proportion. Not everyone who possesses this, which I have said, a possession, and the 'existing things' interpreted allegorically and the 'wealth', holds it in the same way, but to each according to his ability it is distributed.

If, for example, a trainer provides food to athletes and to those around the contest—for he also has others like bodyguards—he gives to each according to a proportion: to one athlete seven pounds of meat—and this is his portion—to another four; and to the one not competing, he gives two. Thus, a portion is given to each according to his power and his capacity. In this way also the parable of the talents in the Gospel occurred. He gave to each of his slaves his own silver, 'to each according to his own ability, to the one five, to the other two, and to the other one' (Matthew 25:15).

Since a more human expression is sometimes used, you know that there are things called sensible comforts for prayers, not only for eating, but also for removing sorrows; and these, therefore, are the spiritual nourishments. And someone receives in order to be glad, and receives a 'portion' so that it may remain with him. He is not only gladdened and fed and drinks from a brief encounter, but also continuously. For he continues drinking from the spring and the water which Jesus gives, and it remains with him. For he has within himself a spring having become a source for eternal life.

And again: 'Open your eyes and be filled with bread' (Isaiah 55:1). The one who opens the eyes of the 'inner man' 'shall be filled with bread'. And the loaves, therefore, thus remain like 'the spring which changes into eternal life'. And this has become useful by way of history, when the widow in Sarepta of Sidon, having only a few drachmae, fed Elijah and she herself had nothing, until prosperity came from the rain (1 Kings 17:14). For he will not remember many of the days of his life, because God distracts him with the joy of his heart. It was necessary in the day of his life to remember many things after these, those who are diligent in these things.

title: The Corruption of Choice and Wealth
english: Something greater happens. He does not remember many things, but has hope only for the present, saying, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13). Therefore, is this what it means that 'God distracts him' (Ps 39:6)? He distracts him in these things, since he does not want to acquire the preceding things, nor does he labor for the taking up of them. So that the soul does not become motionless, other things are given to it. And I said this at the beginning of the book, when I had [it]: 'God gave a wicked distraction.'

Therefore, the ascent: 'that he does not remember many of the days of his life, because God distracts him in the joy of his heart' (Ps 39:6). To live according to philosophy and virtue is the chief and true life. And men do not remember many things, nor do they do much regarding that; they attend only to those who distract them and bring pleasant things, and they strive only about those things which they collect. But it was necessary to remember many things of those which will be useful to his life truly.

And here, then, is the common life, according to which we feel, according to which we have the soul yoked to the body, and according to which irrational animals move and perceive. The divine [life], according to reason and contemplation, is the particular [life] of this man. Therefore, does he not remember this? He does not remember those things contributing to this life, if he has something futile.

Again, here 'heart' for us is the true mind, which sees God. For instance, the saint says 'with boldness' to God: 'my heart was not stuck to me through scandal' [sic]. Again, others have 'fleshly hearts, in which the Spirit of the living God writes.' And he says 'fleshly' meaning those receptive to the writing of the Spirit. It is also possible, according to the literal sense, that he rejoices in his own heart. For he desired to have a heart feeding on pleasure.

One must take the words toward those speaking. If the speaker is wise, one must listen to them wisely. If, being wise, he personifies another face and brings it appropriately to that man, one must again listen to the conversation in that [person]. Since the apostle himself says: 'whether we eat or whether we drink, we neither lack nor exceed' (1 Cor 10:31), whether we are Christians or wise.

Or 'slaves of Christ', we have neither addition nor subtraction from the eating of anything still. But when he says, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13), it is the same scribe, the same one speaking, but not from his own person, not as an apostle speaks, but he took the persona of those saying that beyond this present life, there is no life after these things.

It is an evil that I saw under the sun (Eccl 1:9), and it is much among men; a man, to whom God will give wealth and substance and glory. These are held by evils; and this [evil] I 'saw under the sun' (Eccl 1:9) and especially it abounds among men. And in irrational animals one finds difference; not all horses are so loved as those standing by for contests or for wars. And likewise with donkeys and dogs.

But the difference is great concerning man. For those things indeed act differently. That kind of resting... is the one being expelled. Here, however, choice is a distracted choice, a choice unable to judge what is profitable and what is not profitable; knowledge is an error, to suppose that one is able to produce something from wealth and glory among men, when he sinks from opposites, from injustice and poverty. It is therefore great, since it is taken through choice. And it seems to take that which is neither good nor bad; but it does not bear this evil which one is able to take.

If he has a right thought, it seems that the 'man' has something advantageous compared to the whole race of men. The woman is not so as the man, nor the boy as the one who has come to manhood. If then the 'man' carries these things well, those who are inferior to the man have much more. 'There is' [for him], he says, 'wealth and glory', and he has nothing more of these. He used to have more of them. The wise man, if he has 'wealth', uses the wealth differently than the many-man; the one having 'glory' does not think greatly upon the glory, but also adorns it along with himself. Joseph once had glory, and his own virtue adorned it. And the other wise men did this according to us. But he who has [thought] about the walls and otherwise about the passers-by, caring for them little, that one founders in these things.

title: The Illusion of Control over Wealth
english: And in shipwrecks, one bears neither poverty well, nor wealth, nor glory; from which it is evident that these things, by the very word, are indifferent. For if anyone is able to use them well and for good, by the very word they are neither good nor evil. They are able to have a good use and a useful use, a graspable and praiseworthy one. And it is not surprising if we say this.

And that Egyptian whom they say, the Trismegistus, says that the wise light does not release fate; it is not under necessity, nor is it under the world, but it has become above the heaven; the intellect of the visible things has become above. Therefore they say that the foolish men are under it. Thus, the one who has ascended above human life and is able to say, 'I look not at the visible things, but at the invisible things' (2 Cor 4:18), [knows] that the visible things are temporary, but the invisible are eternal; he is not weakened by them, nor does wealth lift him up, nor does poverty sink him, nor does he seem to have acquired a great evil from a lack of glory. And from the honor and fame of the many, he does not consider himself to have anything.

But what of the ascent? They are rich and glorified in the 'wisdom of this age and of the rulers of this age that are passing away' (1 Cor 2:6). These do not rightly use either glory or prudence. And because of this, they are examined in great sin. For the wise man, even if he lacks one of these, conducting himself magnanimously, is not under evil; he is not at all sick but is healthy, and according to virtue he is healthy.

'Wealth' and 'possessions'—hear thus: as mostly 'possessions' is said of movable things; they even call them treasures. And not only these has this one acquired, but also 'wealth' in property, in estates, in lands, in houses. Toward wealth, therefore, both possessions and glory are given to him. But toward the intellect, it is said, that often someone will know in a false name and will be glorified in glory and in this...

To those thinking highly of themselves, believing they are wise and seeming to be prudent, and that they are not 'mastered by these things' (Luke 12:20); sometimes they obtain what they desire. And it seems to them that 'nothing of theirs is lacking to the soul' (Luke 12:21), thinking they have acquired all 'wealth' of the soul and all 'glory', yet they do not have the power to use them.

Take for me someone who has grasped a great position, but has fallen into misfortune, such that he is no longer progressing; the power of the position is of no use to him. And indeed, we have known such people many times.

To bring this to a point: it is to find a man who is rich, as it has been said allegorically, and yet they have nothing more. No one receives them, no one praises them, and they do not bring profit. And we have known many such men who are learned: observing that something is necessary, and seeing how they are. And there is nothing lacking to his soul from all things which he desires, and God does not permit him to eat from it. Nothing of what he desires is added to him. This he says, that God has not given him power [over them] empty, even if he uses them as he wishes, because he does not rightly satisfy the desire.

Thus the rich man, remembered with Lazarus (Luke 16:19), had everything, and 'possessions and wealth and glory' (Luke 16:19). And he received 'to master' them there, but after this, a deprivation of them occurred, and also of the pleasure upon them; and the one who heard: 'Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you (Luke 12:20). But what you have prepared, to whom will it belong?'

Others, having these things abundantly and very richly, are not permitted to be filled by them; they are prevented from having enjoyment, either through sickness or through some other circumstance. Because a stranger man eats him; and indeed this is also futility and sickness. These things, the 'wealth' which he accompanied, the 'possessions' eat him. And this happens in many ways; sometimes he falls to robbers and his wealth is taken from him. Many times the one summoned by the king...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Multiplicity of Days and Virtue
english: It is taken away, and his own things go to others and are overpowered by someone, and another enjoys those things which he himself worked for. By way of comparison: many have often used things which others have written about with words, not being of their own opinion or glory. Often indeed wise men find books, into which others have labored, and both they and others are nourished by them and are glorified, when they are able to overturn them.

"And this too is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Vanity is the not-retaining and not-enjoying of one's own. If a man should beget a hundred, and live many years and a multitude, because his days shall be many. He has said the external pursuits for men: "wealth, possessions, glory". Then he says also concerning childbearing: it becomes a great sickness. And he has used an excess: "if someone should beget a hundred".

No one at all begets a hundred. Let us say, even if someone is able to beget a hundred from various women; even this provides him no more. For kings indeed become fathers of many children, and this will not prevent deaths. For if he does not have one child, he certainly fails; and he does not have more than this, and even if he has a thousand; for they are not certainly saved in the wars. And he shall live many years.

Appropriately he has said such things, "wealth, possessions, glory" and the others. And he says the bodily goods. Even if someone is not born in sorrows and lives many years, since his life has remained a long time, it is vain, having the promise only until the present life. Because of this, he strives in vain.

But what about the comparison? If someone through instruction begets many and strives to have a long-lasting glory in life, he does not become unchangeable. It is possible to be taken away from the children; for example, this Arius who among us begot many according to teaching and imitation of life. For indeed all were almost by him, and they were turned away, and all left him, and he did not have other men hating him as those begotten by him.

A multitude shall be his days of years. This he says: "he lived a thousand years of days". A multitude of days has become his. But the many-dayed life will benefit him nothing, since thus he receives it according to this time measured by the sun.

Another becomes long-lived upon the good earth, and the multitude of days benefits him. Indeed, it is said in the manner of a promise: 'I will fill him with length of days.' If it is 'better to depart and be with Christ,' then he who remains in the body laments much time, saying, 'Woe, that my sojourning has been lengthened' (Job 7:7); how then is the long-liver and the multitude of days given in the manner of a blessing? This is what it means: whatever years a man may live in this life, they are written down; and the multitude of days will not benefit him at all. For sometimes in the multitude of his days, more sins of his are found and many transgressions.

But he, having those days increasing, preparing the sunrises of the sun of righteousness, as was said a little before, possesses an enjoyment of the things above that exceeds being under the sensible sun. To whatever extent one has approached virtue, he has been enlightened by it. And the days become many in proportion to how much virtue holds sway. If he turns away from this life, he has a multitude of days from this [life]. Thus we call the days those illuminated by the sun of righteousness. And just as regarding the sensible days, a multitude is said of the earth being often circumscribed and... many times the solar cycle... so also [with] virtue... according to itself. That is to say: from life with virtue, one becomes long-lived, long-lasting, and blessed. If he tests these days in virtue, he will not desire to remain for other years. If the vain [life] should turn away from life, since he has hope in God, he becomes [victorious] over all of them, and it is vain for him to live many years. For many years are written down, but the blessed life is greater; it is eternal.

I wish to bring forward the apostolic [view], which some seem to think is according to history. 'Piety,' he says, 'is profitable for all things, having the promise of life, both of the present and of the one to come' (1 Timothy 6:19). When he says 'of the present,' he does not mean this one, concerning which the apostle says, 'If in this life we have hope only' (1 Corinthians 15:19), but the [life] able to exist here according to virtue, concerning which anyone might say it is 'in part.' Because
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Goodness of the Unborn
english: The blessed ones receive this life from that source, which is clearly shown by the words: 'He who believes in me has eternal life' (John 6:47), and 'This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Him whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 17:3). The promise of piety does not possess this life alone—that is, to live blessed here, to live here in the practical and contemplative life—but it also receives this life as the whole receives a part, just as the 'through a mirror' receives the 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12), if something is eternal or if something is long-lasting.

But another life does not receive this temporal life; I say this to those who think it is only this. For they said, 'hoping in this life alone', 'let us eat and drink' (Luke 12:19). And even if something is received in this way, it is not the long-lasting life. They go 'to the lake of fire' (Matt 25:41) and 'have a great penalty of fire' (Matt 25:46), where they have become part of the lot of death, clearly giving judgments against this life. And his soul will not be filled with goodness, and even a burial did not happen to him.

As it has happened, he says, 'wealth and possessions and glory'; he is not immersed in these. Just as he who loves wants to have even more silver and other things, so also he who wants to live luxuriously. For he does not yet want to encounter death. And his ascent is this: whoever is glorified as wise having 'falsely named' 'knowledge', still wants to be more greatly glorified. If he lives according to 'falsely named knowledge', he wished to always have it thus. And even a burial did not happen to him.

He says that 'he lived many years of descent'. A thousand years happened, filled with all things pleasant, he misses nothing; and often without burial he is cast away. 'Better the corpse than this', in which nothing pleasant existed; nor did the shroud have wealth, nor possessions, nor was he glorified, and it is better than this, because he has not experienced any of these at all. This is [applied] to the literal sense. But as an ascent, this is that he has become wealthy in many of those things, yet he did not find the reputation that describes the former life. He says, therefore: 'From the house of your God I will destroy the carved images and the bronze; I will set your burial [as a place]'. Some [say] thus...

Again, he says, 'I will set your burial as a carving,' and not 'I will destroy' these things. And when it is profitable for your soul, you set your burial as a theme. For he baptizes and buries together with the destroyed ones. Indeed, after 'I will set your burial,' he says, 'Judah, keep your feasts.' Therefore, in a feast, one strives for prayers.

He of old, being filled with carving and casting in a tomb, was cast so as to be 'buried with Christ' (Rom 6:4). Therefore, he has called to make it a feast, to do what is necessary; for a feast is nothing other than doing what is required, but we add to it this or that toil. Toward the upward leading, then, it is this: he strove much and grew rich, as if living in vanity with a false opinion, not knowing with clarity, being filled up, 'and there was no burial for him.'

The miscarriage spoke something good for him, that he came in vanity and walks in darkness (Isa 53:9). According to the spoken word concerning the one who grew rich in all possessions, of whom nothing of the abundance remains—not moving, not still, not a glory, not a dignity—and if, having died, he is found outside all these, 'it is a good thing the miscarriage for this one,' which is the one who has not been fully tested by this life.

And toward such an upward leading, it should be taken thus, as it was also said previously regarding the little: 'it was good for him, if he had not been born.' Therefore, it is good for those more [blessed], those who are still leading lives and those who have died, who have not yet been born. Because he came in vanity and walks in darkness (Isa 53:9).

Other people, when they are well-born and well-reared, having used the things given to them badly, had this vanity; but the miscarriage had even its very birth in vanity; it was conceived not that it might live, not that it might become a fetus, but that the womb might immediately perish, immediately as the conception occurred. In darkness, therefore, again, he did not come to men; he was not known, that 'in vanity he came and in darkness he walks' (Isa 53:9). He did nothing, nor thought, nor knew anything of human things. And because of this, as he came with ignorance and through not having experienced these things, so again he walks. Much is there concerning which the word is, and it is sought by many who are unclear as to whether, if the conceptions occur, in order that...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Famine of Jerusalem and the Mother's Choice
english: That men may be born—even if it is up to God whether to give a child or not, and whether to be for a long time or a short time—how can it not be brought about for certain ends, and not be wasted? And even this, having been done, lives for two or three hours; but let us say ten years. Do these things not happen in this way? Are these 'judgments' not resembling 'the great deep'? We only know in the whole that it has not happened in vain; even if it had possessed vanity in not being born or not being reared, especially our born one does not do these things in vain.

Why is that unknown thing? Because we have human calculations. But it happens for salvation and for this, which God gives to each one. The soul not giving the same due renders all these things void. For if it is sown together, all these things are vain. But the ends of things happen by the judgment of God; and God says to give children. And if ever indeed men ask children from him, the gifts of God are judged together. If any of them happened to have many, he prays by word, but by the word of wisdom and knowledge, that he may have gifts. [Garbled text]. Following the ascent, then, that some were born—perhaps the daughters of divine teaching—to be received, so that they might be brought forth, and immediately they were harmed.

Thus also that which is said in the Gospel was lifted up. Concerning much tribulation coming, it says: 'Woe to those with child and to those nursing' (Luke 23:29). She who has in the womb, receiving the tribulation and not bringing forth, is harmed. And that was received in vain. And they indeed were born, but they did not become perfect, but they bore the nursing ones; and again, quickly, the soul having become into tribulation, they were harmed, having virtue newly born, having encountered first in catechesis. It is possible even to take this as history; the coming of that tribulation mentioned in the Gospel required flight. As for the whole, take it toward the spoken word: those having in the womb were being hindered, using a sharp run, and were being seized. And the war against the Hebrews is hinted at, even the Roman war. She having in the womb is not able to suffer evil or...

Whether in fleeing or in not being nourished like another nursing woman. The oppression of the famine and the great evils are thus pointed out in the laments, because even 'pitiful women' (Lam 4:10) ate 'their own children'. For she did not permit others, not being pitiful, to use simply the food that was being found, even if it were his child; but it signifies the oppression of the hardship and the sparing of the necessary things.

The ones sharing in the misery, therefore, ate their own children, not only toward the children, but also toward others. Such a thing is remembered in that Mary, in the accounts concerning the fall of Jerusalem. She was fond of children—and she had only a child—and she was also among the well-to-do and the very wealthy. Much, I think, of prosperity she had used for nourishment; at times she bought a goat or some meat. And by the plunderers during the insurrection and by hand through the wars, there became a lack. And if the insurrectionists had perceived the smoke, they were entering and casting down the meals.

Taking therefore her child—and he was about three years old—she gave him certain words, in which she also said this: 'It is more profitable for you to be eaten by me or to exchange something bad and endure slavery from your enemies. Go then and become my food.' And having slaughtered, she saw him. A little later the insurrectionists entered and she did not allow them to enter, but she was saying to them: 'Come, eat even the half.' And she as if conquered them.

And in darkness his name shall be covered, and indeed he did not see the sun and did not know rest, because of this one over this one. This says, that this one is nothing at all. And the 'darkness' denotes the unknown 'name', the ignorance of him because of not being known. He came to us neither perceived nor having been led in a dark way. The: 'and indeed he did not see the sun.' He will not even perceive; he had no other rest. For to see the sun is to behold. He did not see therefore this one; and if he did not have the perception of this sense, it is evident that he did not even of the others. And I do not say this at all: 'by this one over this one', the one who was beyond the one who had led them to wealth.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Hyperbolic Language and the Necessity of Love
english: And [he] had glory and much instruction and a long life, because having been tested by all these things, he became an outcast and was not even quickly worthy. He had nothing from these things through his wound; that one did not even suffer the same things as himself.

Regarding the turning back: 'and even the sun did not know him' (Matt 26:24). In agreement, you again take the turning back, because many, having been tested by the pleasures of those pursuing glory, another was not even tested at their beginning. This one is better than that one. For that one, for the sake of which he strove and possessed, 'he will give a word' and will be punished. But this one does not endure this, not even having entered the beginning through human thoughts or having had a trial of them.

Again, to consider a man who has died even in ignorance to be better than all, but [one] who has judged all in pseudonymous knowledge. Peter alludes in the second epistle: 'it was better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, or to have known and to have turned back from the holy commandment handed down to them' (2 Pet 2:21). For he does not say at all that it is good to not have known the way of righteousness, but rather it is better not to have known than to have known and to despise it.

He has not said other things as regarding Judas, just as the Savior [said]: 'it was good for him, if he had not been born' (Matt 26:24). It was good for him, if he had not been called; if he had not been called, he would not have betrayed. It would not have been otherwise good for Saul, if he had not been king; for he did not fall among the lawless, among whom he fell after becoming king. And what did he live for a thousand years of descents, and he did not see goodness? If he lived a thousand years of descents, then he was a father of a thousand children: 'if a man begets a hundred' (John 10:40). To live, then, as a name consistent with begetting, let him take. But it would not be a conception of seed if, without the producing of offspring, there were no sowing of it; thus, not even...

These things would not have happened without a soul coming. According to the union that occurs, there are two causes: the marriage of the body, and the 'descent' of the soul. It is said similarly. Again, they say in this way 'descents' are cycles of years. Each year has a certain beginning, which we call his 'descent'.

Even if someone has become many-years from the multitude of years, he continued in the life which he had with diligent care, which makes those pursuing him compassionate; he gains nothing from this, so that becoming a thousand years might be equal to living a thousand years of descent; here 'cycle' is used in order to be. But how is it according to the explicit text and improbable and impossible? It is not improbable nor impossible; it has been spoken in a hyperbolic manner. And things spoken by way of hyperbole are not improbable and impossible—impossible at times, but not improbable. For someone will say thus: if a man is able to beget ten, he is able to beget a hundred, and to live so many years, if he lived fifty. The former, Methuselah, lived near a thousand. Therefore, the word is a hyperbole for the sake of emphasis, exaggerating the truth.

When the height of the cities constructed by those before Israel who possessed the land is spoken of, saying, 'we saw cities there with walls, whose walls [reached] even to the heaven', it was spoken hyperbolically. And the apostle also knew the logic of hyperbole and the use of the name. 'And still, by way of hyperbole, I say to you: if I have all knowledge and know all the mysteries, but do not have love, I benefit nothing' (1 Cor 13:2). For it is not profitable to know knowledge and all the mysteries without divine love. 'If we have all the faith so as to remove mountains, not having love, the greatness of the faith is nothing' (Matt 17:20). He says love is greater and [that it is] faith; and he gives it [the power] to say the mountains are removed; this is not lying, even if it exaggerates.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Life as a Shadow
english: the truth, so as to encounter unbelief. And he says again: 'and Ahaziah was swift in doing as the watchers in the field' (1 Kings 22:38). He was fast. And according to allegory, often the life of men and their polity is called a sea. Here, waves are able to signify what happens to man. And he says that regarding the judgments happening to him, 'it ascends even unto the heavens' and 'it descends even unto the depths' (Psalm 36:9).

[Gaps] ... in the following year ... [Gaps] ... what is superfluous to man? ... so in general regarding man he says, [Gaps] ... of the things ... [Gaps] ... when [Gaps] ... [Gaps] ... here also regarding [Gaps] ... the Jews were stronger ... [Gaps] ... the words of God and ... 'a part of him'. And those from the Greeks who believed were called ... [Gaps] ... the Jews being such as being a holy commonwealth and the others, but having made the things called [Gaps] subject to those on whom he was called ... and so this is to say 'what is superfluous', if first someone is called and ... [Gaps] ... he took it for himself ... [Gaps] ... [Gaps] ... and he speaks about the conduct and life here. This living we have while being in the flesh and passing through this. It is under time, it is under the number of days. But the truly living is eternal; and such a life is both eternal and without end. He speaks therefore about the life here, the life in heaven. And he made them in shadows; for who will announce to man what will be after him under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:9). The life of men, which they lead here, is shadowy. You have in the Gospel said by the Savior: 'Seek', he says, 'first the righteousness...'

"...and the kingdom of God, and all these things will be set before you." It is impossible for a shadow to be without a pre-existing body. There must be a body so that a shadow may thus follow it. Therefore, the life here is a shadow, being a consequence of a preceding life, which the life occurring here follows. For this reason it is said, "our days are as a shadow." And Job also said previously, "the life of men on the earth is a shadow." The life on the earth, or the material life, the temporal, the one in the flesh, this is a "shadow" of the life above.

It is a possible thing, an easy thing, a productive thing. So also the apostle, wishing to show the shadowy life, said, "If in this life we have only hoped, we are more to be pitied than all men" (1 Cor 15:19). Let a man, having some hope, attend to a shadow appearing to help him; in a palace, if someone perceives the face of a king not present, will the shadow or the appearance benefit him? For it is not possible for that which can be present to him beside a true king who rules according to laws, to be [the shadow itself]. Therefore our life is shadowy. But having known this, beloved, that this life is shadowy, attend to it as to something not permanent, as to something dependent on another; and in this, observe that there is another life which the shadowy life follows, and live and act according to that.

For thus "one is able to please God." Because of "who will announce to man" (Eccl 1:3) what follows him while he still exists under the sun, all divination is refuted from that source, all human prophecy. For "under the sun" is not in vain. For those having ascended above the sun of the Son and having approached the sun of righteousness, as it is said of them that "they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father," it is not possible to announce "what will come after," or what receives them. And as I have said and now will say: we say that we have ignorance of the judgments of God, since they happen to be "unsearchable. The judgments of God are very deep" (Rom 11:33). And the abyss is incomprehensible or difficult to comprehend. And let it be said that even if some were judged by a most righteous king in a dream, each according to his own sin, we all know that they were judged justly, though not to this extent...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Good Name and the True Light
english: For what reason? We have this to say even here. Again, many among the rulers turned toward private interests. This same Ecclesiastes says: 'I saw slaves on horses and rulers riding about' (Eccl 10:7), and we cannot say for what reason he has this. But we can say in general that the things of men fall away. If, however, surpassing these, we become heavenly, no longer observing the temporal and apparent things, then we will lift ourselves to God, being able to know such things as follow after these.

For each one receives a reward according to his practice and his work. This is said regarding God by the Psalmist: 'You will render to each according to his works' (Ps 62:11). And even if the works are manifest, we do not trust in what kind of disposition is performing them. Moreover: 'And he made them in shadow.' The upward leading? He says this: 'Those having shone like the sun in the kingdom of their own Father' lived in the true days. In a manner of promising, he spoke concerning someone: 'I will fill him with length of days' (Dan 12:2). Indeed, these long days occurring toward the light of the truth are not shadowy; they are the prototypes. But the days which we can still receive while surrounded by flesh are shadowy.

Then one knows 'in part,' when 'the perfection has not yet come' (1 Cor 13:12), when he possesses the 'earnest of the Spirit' (Eph 1:14) and the light of the truth. Someone 'made these days in shadow,' but he did not know what would be behind him, whether he would surpass the shadow or fall down by it. And so that we may take the view from another example: the Jews have come to be in shadow, 'in the shadow' of days, not in the days themselves. For Moses, speaking the previous and true days, interprets: 'This is your life and this is the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5).

But the love toward God occurring 'from all the soul and from all the disposition' does not work an increase of these days. For many diligent and God-fearing men were quickly transferred from life, and others, the most mediocre, lived long. For who will announce to man what will be behind him under the sun? 196 Being of doubt...

One must take the word in two ways, so that this is both 'what shall be announced to him under the sun' (Ecclesiastes 1:9) and 'who else under the sun is able to announce'. Both are true. Furthermore, what is the leading up? This leading up is this: for both the man and the one striving to truly possess what is pleasant to him, [it is asked] 'who will announce to him, what will be after him under the sun'. It can be said here of the things that shine forth, those that lead up from the shadow, and those that guide from the temporal into the eternal. It is also possible to take this regarding the 'shadow' of righteousness, that 'who will announce to him, what will be to them under the sun', while still approaching righteousness. For he is no longer under the 'sun of righteousness' himself, having surpassed the shadow and having become in that truth seeing it 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12).

A good name is preferred over oil, and the day of death over a day of birth. It exhorts to attend to a good reputation. For it has been said: 'A good reputation is praised by bones' (Prov 22:1). And we are accustomed to say that the one attending to virtue has acquired a good name, and the one living shamefully receives a bad name. Therefore, one is exhorted to attend to reputation. For this name, which seems to be sweet like oil, is good. Furthermore, is the spoken word clear? Those living well in life seem to be praised—but this can be with slander; such as the rich man remembered after Lazarus, and the one who heard: 'Fool, in this night they require your soul from you (Luke 12:20). But what you have prepared, what will it be?' Therefore, you prefer and choose this name of the seemingly good oil. But it is possible to take up the beautiful name, to make use of the chosen name of God. In order that the name not be bare, the good name consists according to virtue. And someone acquires this with toil and pain and sweat. But that which becomes sweet by chance often happens and is outside of their own striving. This is what the saint rejects, saying: 'Let not oil that sins anoint my head', which they think is sweet and oils themselves, but he says let it not be for me. For not every reputation is praiseworthy. The name here can be equal to reputation. Many are well-spoken of, who are able to exhaust others, [claiming] that they are rich, that they are rulers. This...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Mourning
english: Therefore the name is not for the sake of mercy. For there is nothing else of mercy. But that which is truly to be chosen and brings to the possessor something beyond the pleasures of life is the true name.

Similarly he speaks concerning days, that those truly bringing the things of importance according to the inner man and those leading an 'unblemished life' (βίον ἀκηλίδωτον) have a good name. And this is that which is beyond mercy, beyond the pleasures.

But some acquire this name not from works, not from life, but from the pride and haste of certain [people]. That name is not more choice than mercy. One must have something to be pitied; but with this mercy, if he makes his life right, the true name, more choice, is to be preferred.

And the day of his death is preferred over the day of his birth. The day of birth is the beginning of tribulation and ill-doing. The day of birth introduces man into life, where there are many evils and bad things; but the day of death imposes an end upon the struggling life.

Therefore he who does not attend to the things at hand nor thinks great things upon them, but knowing that 'it is better to be dissolved with Christ' (κάλλιον ἀναλύσαντα σὺν Χριστῷ εἶναι), prefers the day of death over the day of birth. For the one is the beginning of many evils, but the other is the end and the description of the evils.

And the evils we call here those of struggle, the indifferent things: poverty, vainglory, and those related to these. It is good to go into a house of mourning or to go into a house of wine (Ecclesiastes 7:4). Fluidity of character does not occur where mourning is. For there, boasting and laughing are turned away; this misfortune does not allow this to happen.

And at times, when we guard ourselves from misfortune through displeasure toward the unfortunate and the suffering, we are even permitted to appear joyful. But in the house of wine, what happens is contrary, bringing lust and songs, being a symptom of a coarse life.

Therefore, it is 'good' for the wise 'to go into a house of mourning or into a house of wine' (Ecclesiastes 7:4). This drinking together, when no evil is brought, brings neither good nor bad. Or is it so that we might not receive 'mourning' that is false? But that which the Savior makes blessed.
And regarding the spoken word, let us say that to be with those undergoing misfortune does not harm. The house of mourning, declaring our nature entirely, provides a reminder that we...

Not only the first ones are unhappy, but we also possess mourning; for mourning is common. But the ascent: the house is one of mourning, where there are doctrines of moral sins and the punishments upon them. For hearing these things, men both mourn and lament over themselves. So what, then, is the good in mourning? For it brings blessedness. For 'blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted' (Matt 5:4). Mourning is a prelude and a beginning of comfort. But the Savior does not bless those who mourn in just any way. For sometimes they also fall away, even while the word says: 'Do not weep for one dead, nor mourn him; but weep with a weeping for the one departing from the presence of the Lord, because he will not return again' (Luke 23:28). This one is worthy of weeping. It is not necessary to mourn the one dead, but the one dead having fallen away from blessedness and eternal life. In many ways, one can mourn himself having become lost in sins, if he perceives it. And he is blessed, the one mourning himself, having made himself worthy of mourning and having fallen from the blessed life, so that he may be comforted. And he mourns others also, when he is a lover of children. Thus indeed Paul was saying: 'Not having entered, I shall mourn many.' 'Many' he says, those 'not having repented.' This one mourning does not mourn himself, but the others having been made dead, or rather his own children through discipline in any way.

And the house signifies a certain state and an ascent, not a place. He knew this, the end of every man, and the living one will give good to his heart. The one going into a 'house of mourning' knows that 'the end of every man' is to die. And if he knows that he will die, he will not think much of it, nor will he consider it a matter of great importance if he possesses such things which he is able to cast off having died—wealth, glory, rank—according to 'do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied, for he will not take all things in his dying' (Prov 23:17-18). And the living one will give good to his heart. To the living belongs the hunting of what seems good to himself. This is the pleasant. For the one dead and enduring what is worthy of being mourned does not 'give good in his heart.' But if a beautiful and good thing is snatched away from life, the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Wrath vs. Human Mirth
english: Truly he finds 'good' for himself, 'entering into the joy of the Lord' (Matt 8:12). But if he is foolish, there too he 'endures weeping' (Matt 8:12). 'For there is the weeping and the gnashing of teeth' (Matt 8:12). And it is possible even to call the living 'the one living according to God'. Such were those around Abraham, concerning whom it has been said: 'God is not of the dead, but of the living' (Matt 22:32). The one truly living, the one having the blessed life, finds good for his own soul.

For the ascent: 'he knew this [is] the end of every man' (Eccl 3:2). The foolish man is called a man according to a different meaning, as it has been said: 'but you indeed as men are dying' (Eph 4:5), and: 'for where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not men?' (Jas 3:14). The one having cast off this life, by which he is a real man, mourns blessedly. But the living one, by desiring such an ascent and life, preserves the sweetness for himself; he does not seek the salvation after these things, that which is made straight through much toil. 'For through many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter into the kingdom of the heavens' (Acts 14:22), and: 'being afflicted in all things' (2 Cor 4:8), these have no sweetness. The one having mourned, therefore, 'knew the end of every man' (Eccl 3:2). Thus indeed he mourns as it is described of him, of the living, of the one being published.

The living one will not, therefore, simply give the good, but toward 'his own heart' being fond of love. A good passion [is] over laughter, because in the wickedness of man he will be angry. And from what is at hand it is possible to see this: if anyone has obedient ones, such as children or slaves, when he thus becomes angry and is passionate toward them so as to prevent their wickedness, this 'passion' is 'good', not passion absolutely, but the father toward a child, the guardian toward those being cared for. 'Because in the wickedness of man he will be angry' (referring to the one seeking laughter, who becomes a fool there where the jesters are); but the one having 'passion' against those doing such things and will be angry for himself, whenever a calculation or a matter such as this comes to him, as we said recently, that he is angry for his own sake.

[The text begins mid-sentence] ...setting aside the heart because of the wickedness of man. Or, is it for the purpose of leading [one] upward? Having read the divine writings and having known how God is indignant against sinners and that he 'stirs up wrath' (Ps 7:11), which the holy man was entreating, saying: 'Do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger' (Ps 6:6)—this wrath is not better than living with virtue; rather, if one is worthy to be punished, it is preferable for him to be rebuked through wrath or to be disciplined by that punishment. For he who is able to punish rages before the actual punishing.

Do we not hear in the Scripture that a threat lies in store against sinners? If the thing announced is wrath, what then is a threat? And in the threat is the wrath, not in the fulfillment of the threat. Or, in the punishment, is the wrath not greater? But he does not speak of this as a good thing, if anyone is tested by it, but rather that if wrath is released, sins increase, so that punishment may follow. Therefore, the 'good' is 'wrath over laughter.' That is, to find pleasure in evils. 'Because in the wickedness of man he shall be made good.' Laughter is made good in the wickedness of man; and the maker of laughter brings wickedness to himself and to others.

Thus, he who hunts for pleasures is made good in the wickedness of man, he who prefers softness to a rigorous life. The face of this laughter seems to be cheerful in wickedness. But if we speak regarding the one being raged against, that the thing appearing in the threat is not a wickedness opposed to virtue, but a wickedness that punishes those who err, concerning which it is also written in the prophet Amos: 'If there is wickedness in the city, which the Lord did not make?' (Am 3:6). There is no evil occurring in a city by nature without God. The heart of the wise is in a house of mourning, and the heart of the foolish is in a house of mirth (Eccl 7:4). Behold, he has shown how the face of 'wrath' is preferable to that of 'laughter' among the things being taken; for indeed, the heart of the wise is more toward a house...

title: The Rebuke of the Wise vs. the Laughter of Fools
english: A person is driven by grief or toward a house of drinking and laughter. The comparison made is such that they choose some things and flee others in many ways, one of which is from those who choose. The wise man chooses virtue, piety, 'to please God', and strives for piety, even if he must die. But the many-sided man, the fool, does not choose these.

From the things chosen, virtue is preferred, because the wise choose it, not the coarse, not the exhausted, not the fool. And from the facts, again the comparison is taken, the beautiful thing said by those judging and comparing. The necessary thing is taken when we say that the soul is more excellent than the body, and it is more fitting to care for it rather than the body. From the matter, toward which the choice and comparison happen, the precious thing is taken, since the soul is more precious. He who is sparing and caring of it cares for the precious and the better according to truth.

And there is also when the preference happens from the things accompanying. Thus it is not necessary to prefer living simply over dying. For even if someone prefers living over the one about to die through clamor or the justice of a judge or something else pursuing Christianity and the truth, it is for a little while. For if he does not die by the murderer, sometimes a disease having seized him interrupts life; it has difference only in time, that he who is immediately subject to the wrath of a judge dies, but to be destroyed by disease, life's end is uncertain, when. However, this is not for an infinity, but in more time he may remain. And thus the judgment happens from the singularity or the speed of the matter.

It is good to hear the rebuke of a wise man rather than the songs of fools. It seems to many that the rebuke from the wise should be avoided, especially when they are lovers of sin. For he having the desire to enjoy and to sin avoids the one forbidding these things. He who has no opinion at all rejoices in flatteries; he wants rather to hear the songs of flattery than the words of rebuke. For it is the part of a wise man to love the one rebuking. For it is said in Proverbs: but the impious and the evil man hates the one rebuking. For he says: 'He who rebukes the impious will be blamed and himself.' For he blames himself, the one [rebuking] the impious...

For the impious man is to be rejected and forbidden. And just as a physician who subjects those unable to be cured by cutting or cautery to such things is not a physician, but an ignorant physician, so he who reproves the incorrigible reproaches himself more, for he provokes them to speak against him.

And they show that one having such a fault does not know whom to reprove and whom not to. Such is the rebuke of the wise over the laughter of fools. Flatterers sing in a certain way; even if they speak moral words, they wish more to please than to benefit those who hear. Laughter is a word that stirs up pleasure, but rebuke, being corrective and persuading one to cease former works, demonstrates them, making it clear that they are things to be avoided and forbidden.

Is it the wise man who rebukes or the one being rebuked? It is the rebuke of the wise, not that which he himself undergoes, but that which he imposes on others. If you wish to take it as 'the rebuke of the wise' being that which he himself undergoes, that is a violent interpretation, yet he says this: the wise man receiving rebuke corrects himself and casts away those things for which the rebuke happened to him, and this is good for him. But he does not mean this, but rather that which he brings to those worthy of rebuke, so that the saying might be similar to this: 'He who brings wisdom from his lips strikes a heartless man with a rod.'

Just as the sound of thorns under a cauldron is so, such is the laughter of fools. And this too is vanity. For the thorns, when they are burned under a cauldron, produce a great noise. And so the laughter of fools is such, until they produce noises; it is not for the sake of refreshing the soul. If the soul does not laugh, it has not yet reached the point of rebuking. Often in the writings, the cauldron signifies punishment. 'For a east wind shall burn from the face of the countenance upon those inhabiting the land' (Ezekiel 20:45), when the people mocked the prophet, they laughed. Fools do not laugh until they have made a noise and sounds; they are more like jesters. And just as the thorns themselves, being burned under the cauldron, emit a noise, so their laughter is from a scorched, evil soul.

title: The Beginning and End of Wisdom
english: Bringing forward those [things]. Furthermore, the upward leading: 'It is good to hear a rebuke from the wise.' The divine word of the Scriptures is wise, and each one of those guarding it is wise according to God, is God-wise. When therefore one such rebukes, is the effort good or not? And he rebukes well. But many rebuke even regarding not allowing someone to be a buffoon, for the sake of not dancing and doing such things. But the wise man brings forward a check against sin. And the rebuke, being such a thing of the wise, being improving, even if the one being improved is not improved, it is good beyond the folly of the foolish, the punishment of the word and not rebuking. And even if a man is harmed through the folly of the foolish, it is not only a woman or a child.

The worldly cares are indeed thorns, the shameful desires, the unrestrained pleasures. This he says: that such things, which those playing the buffoon think they do with pleasure, are thorns, bringing and coming under punishment. And this is vanity. For they will gain nothing from laughter; as you would say to one living badly: 'It is in vain for you.' For slander carries away the wise and destroys the good disposition of his heart. The 'carries away' is thus: often someone accuses the wise man badly and finds many following him. And if he was not entirely well-disposed and perfect, at times he also is shaken.

Susanna, her wise soul not being carried away, was slandered regarding adultery. And the slander was not being said against one or two false accusers; those ruling the people and judges of such accusations were the accusers. All the people paid attention to them as judges and as those ruling the people. And almost no one was a forger of the slander. When therefore, being God-wise, she perceived that in vain the things of the accusation were for her—for she would not find the one listening—she fled to God and with the spoken word she was silent, but with the mind she cried out: 'O God, the Eternal One, the Knower of hidden things, who knows all things before their being, you know that they testify falsely against me.' Slander did not carry her away, nor did it establish her in misery, but it confirmed her in sobriety. And Joseph likewise. And in the time especially of the persecutions, many...

They were flattered and not driven about. Therefore, the wise one here does not speak of the perfect one, but of the one having the beginning, the new one. Thus we have also understood: 'rebuke the wise, and he will love you'. The perfect wise man is not subject to any rebukes. For when it says, 'the wise will not depart from the mouth of the Most High' (Psalm 115:13), it speaks of the perfect ones here.

Many indeed sacrificed without even having a choice, 'the loss of the straightness of their heart'. For it is possible for toil to drive out a heavy intention not entirely all-powerful. A good end of words concerning his beginning, a good long-suffering concerning a high spirit. The end of the words rather has already something good concerning the beginning of the words.

The one beginning the word, in order that you may take the word here as active, the real one, implicitly has it, if he completes the word, if he acts according to the word. But the one having already arrived at that very end of the words—the end of the word—for which it happens, not toward which the word is. It is said a word so that a thing may be born or so that... [text is garbled/gapped]... they hear, therefore is an end... [text is garbled/gapped]... the word forbids an end... [text is garbled/gapped]... for it has been said, 'by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned' (Matt 12:37), so that the being justified... [text is garbled/gapped]... is the end of the spoken words.

Therefore, of the introduction... [text is garbled/gapped]... for it happens to the one beginning... [text is garbled/gapped]... to be, for which the words. A good long-suffering concerning a high spirit. 'High spirit' he calls the boaster... [text is garbled/gapped]... the Savior did not say... [text is garbled/gapped]... and often it has been said that spirit signifies the mind according to the body, and the Virgin [is] holy in spirit; therefore to love... [text is garbled/gapped]... is to be lofty in spirit. The long-suffering one does not become lofty in spirit, he is not proud. Often, indeed, when instructing someone without sharpening [the intellect] according to the understanding, he approaches long-sufferingly the...
