title: The distinction between future existence and imminent tendency
english: Even if one ascends to the invisible things, since these are nearer and primary, and others lie beyond them and surpass them, he will never cease to know, until he reaches that limit of knowing God as He is. The one who stands over himself is known by knowledge, and he is both a knower and a scientist.

I have said this generally: that often the soul, when it is a plant being cultivated, possesses both terms. It cultivates itself, not cultivating something else; it does not cultivate things outside itself as one cultivating sensible plants; it does not care for something else, but is a technician of plants. For since he is not a knower of what is to come, or how it will be, who will announce it to him? Because of this, 'much is the knowledge concerning man.' No one perceives what is to come; sensation has apprehension of the present things. But the things to come have not yet stood in existence. Therefore, there is no sensory apprehension of the things not yet standing, but a cognitive contemplation; science is that which contemplates what is to come.

Immediately, indeed, so that we may give [an example], some claim to know what happens from fate, yet they do not know the things to come. For unless they take again a sequence, that this star has happened according to this zodiac, they know things that are, not things to come. Even if they sometimes speak prophetically about an eclipse of the sun or moon, they take [the sequence] again, that if this travels and such a state of the stars occurs, this will result. In reality, they take the theory again from the fact that it has often happened thus. For as it will be, who will announce it to him? Some have observed the difference between what is about to be and what is to come. It is said that it is sensorially possible, but they say things as if they were certainties existing and having a sequence in contemplation: 'Behold, I am with you all the days until the end of this age' (Matthew 28:20). He did not say 'I am following' this. For the being is different from the what will be. That which results according to the truth of nature, this...

It will be, but that which is not sensorially present is merely tending to be, yet is capable of existing. Look, I say: has a thunderclap become just now? I do not speak of it as having become, but that which is to be is tending to be; for it is not yet. But that which is to come is entwined with that which has preceded it, if it possesses a cause and a causal reason. I do not say that the thing caused tends to be, but that it will be. For when that of which it is the cause is found to be present, with which its existence is entwined, this will certainly be. Therefore, those things which are to come, no one was able to know, unless God is made manifest, or unless the truth directs the mind to knowledge.

He said thus: 'Behold, I will be with you' (Matthew 28:20), not 'I tend to be.' For I have been sent from you, and from you I exist and will be for all the days of the age. And so that I may speak more clearly, humans use both knowledge and sensation. When the sensible things are not present, there is an apprehension of these things tending to be; nor is it apprehended from elsewhere when the non-present is not sensed, but rather that which has already come into being. But when one has a scientific theory, and imposes it demonstratively upon each problem, he already possesses the knowledge and possesses it as something tending to be. For it does not fail like sensory apprehension.

And indeed, a certain place is attempted that is more sophistical than dialectical, because the sun is above the earth and such a motion of his appears when it is day, when the underlying air is illuminated by him. But when, they say, he is able, we do not know whether he is or is not. And even if we posit that, they say, he is able, we do not know whether he is or is not. For if we posit that he is, we have this by some assumption. But if he does not appear, we do not know whether he exists or does not exist. —I said, then, that the attempt of this is sophistical. Listen: things are accepted according to definitions. Some have defined the sun to be a day-appearing star. And in this way, the 'day-appearing' was taken as the distinction. But distinctions must always exist for the definitions; if, therefore, as a distinction of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Bread of Life and the Cleansing of the Soul
english: The sun is taken to be a day-star; however, if it is not day, it lacks the distinction found in its definition. Therefore, it is unclear whether it is or is not. Having anticipated this, I said that it is a sophism; it is neither a scientific theorem nor a dialectical problem.

There is no man exercising authority in spirit to prevent the spirit that governs all things. According to the immediate and the literal, there is no man who exercises authority in spirit so as to receive the movement of the air as a spirit, that is, the wind. For he does not exercise authority over much that he does not want to be wind, nor can he draw it, nor can he prevent one who would harm a friend. Most are not possessing authority, even if they were excellent pilots, so as to draw a breath parallel to those sailing, nor to stop it when it is most violent and harmful. According to the immediate, then, it is to be taken thus.

Since often the soul of man is called a spirit, the one possessing authority is not such as to make the soul remain or to release it from the living creature. It is held by providence... 'Send your bread upon the face of the waters, for in the multitude of days you will find it; divide it to the seven and also to the eight' (Eccl 11:1ab2a). This wording has nothing to do with the literal. For what is useful for history is the 'bread' which someone has, to send 'upon the face of the waters'? Rather, it makes it useless. Therefore, this wording must be taken for thought alone and for spiritual ascent.

Often in the abundance of divine teachings, the multitude of men is addressed by this name: 'Save me,' he says, 'from many waters, from the hand of the sons of strangers'; 'many waters' has spoken of the 'sons of strangers' of the divine wrath. And again there are many other writings teaching this; it is indeed said that 'God gives upon the water...' and they are not found to be taken according to history. But the multitude of men can signify the 'water.' It is necessary, then, that the 'bread' of salvation, which nourishes the soul, be 'sent' 'upon the face of' such 'water.' This says... to be 'water,' but 'send,' not...

The bread will be found in the abundance of days. For it will sprinkle the water. Again, to lead toward another meaning, this is said: this bread is not a sensible thing, but it is about that which is said, 'the bread of life has descended from heaven.' This bread must be taken after the cleansing of the soul, as 'he who has desired wisdom has kept the commandments, and the Lord will provide it to him.' First, one receives cleansing—'cleanse your soul, make your soul shining'—and thus one finds the bread 'upon the water,' where 'upon' signifies 'after.' And he says, 'Behold, you find this bread in the abundance of your days.' It does not merely 'work' and nourish for the present, but also 'in the abundance of days.' And this is possible because, as many illuminations come from the 'sun of righteousness,' you have a 'multitude of days' according to 'I will fill them with length of days' and 'he shall be long of life.' 'You will find the bread in the abundance of days.' Even more and more, as it 'shines,' you 'find' the bread of truth, the 'bread of life,' so that the sowing of righteousness was the 'water,' and after the sowing of righteousness, 'upon' [the water], you may sow the fruit and the knowledge of the 'light of the true [one].'

Does the praised bread 'work' upon sprinkled 'water'? We do not say 'upon' sprinkled water, but just as we say that one who 'walks in ignorance' and 'darkness' approaches the 'light,' we do not say that those remaining 'in ignorance' and 'unawareness' approach the light; the conjunction dissolves the first [elements]. Likewise, regarding 'Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden,' it is not so that you remain 'heavy laden,' for 'I will give you rest.' And here is the paradox: he who practices sin with pleasure, even if it is the heaviest, does not feel it as a weight, does not 'get laden,' and it does not seem to him to be an evil. But when sin is felt as a weight and a burden, then it 'gets laden' and 'labors' and approaches the 'one who gives rest.' Such is also what is said in Isaiah: 'Egypt has labored, Ethiopia is a merchant'—according to the common [text] it is either 'merchant' or 'merchants'—'and the Sabeans are tall men'—and they also 'labored'; and he immediately says that 'upon you' they shall come.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Assyrian and the Seven Shepherds
english: the weight of the sixth verse
The devil himself is defeated against you. When he approaches and draws near and finds strong ones, then he is destroyed.

Something like this was also mentioned a little ago regarding what was said in Isaiah: 'Before a child is known to call father or mother, he shall take the power of Damascus and the raids of Samaria against Assyria the king' (Isaiah 7:8). It was not a great thing if he 'had taken the power of Damascus,' that is, the nations, and 'having taken the raids of Samaria' he 'would deliver' if the 'Assyrian' had gone away. As if someone holds a territory in the absence of the ruling king and takes it, it is not a great thing, nor is 'peace' secure; for 'coming' that one will avenge the things taken in his absence. But when, in the presence of the defender, it is taken from him, they are strong and, having the deepest 'peace,' they are the ones removing his things.

Therefore he says that 'this peace' is the true one. 'This peace' is when 'the Assyrian, having come into your land,' is defeated, when he is rendered helpless, being unable to 'raid' from the 'land' because of his own weakness. 'And seven shepherds shall arise against him,' he says—the holy ones before the visitation, as it was said, because the Sabbath named 'seven'—'and eight marks of men' after the visitation who believed. These 'bite' and cause him pain. For the wording in the Scripture means this: 'But if you bite and devour one another' (James 2:15-16); and in Habakkuk again concerning this same evil one, it is said that 'suddenly they shall arise, biting him' (Habakkuk 1:5). Contrary to expectation, those from the nations who once 'shall arise' against him cause him pain, 'biting him.'

He therefore says that the holy ones before the visitation 'shall arise against the Assyrian, seven shepherds,' so that you may take all the prophets before the visitation, these patriarchs, as these 'shepherds,' not standing on the number 'seven' which is divided into five and two, but on the mystery of the week. Those who had 'left the Sabbath to the people of God for forty [years]' found 'rest of soul' through Jesus—for 'you shall find rest for your souls' (Matthew 11:29)—these are in the true Sabbath and are named by him through the 'seven.' They are said...

title: The Eightfold Sign and the Rain of the Word
english: The 'eight signs of men' are those who, after the coming of the Savior, have approached the gospel and are toiling and 'biting' the enemy. And regarding his toil, which all those called by the gospel have undergone, the word signifies things differently: at times 'with crushing' of him—'the God of peace will crush Satan' (Rom 16:20)—at other times his toil—the 'biting'—and at other times the undoing of his harm—'for I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you' (Luke 10:19). The 'will not harm' here means 'will not strike.'

For you do not know what will be evil under the earth. If the clouds of rain are filled, they pour out upon the earth. Since you are ignorant of the 'evil upon the earth,' that is, that which is done contrary to the good, or the toil that the 'evil'—that which receives the things men do—has undergone, because of this, do as I command you: 'give a portion to the seven and to the eight'; for from these two scriptures you will 'know' what is being done 'evilly' and what 'evil' is coming against those doing evil. Because of this, 'give a portion to the seven and to the eight.' Moreover, are you then the one 'giving to the seven'? It is not possible otherwise to 'know.' It is as if you say: read then the scripture, for you do not know what you ought to do and what not to do. Because of this, 'know what it is,' what must be done and what must not. Similar to this is 'test all things' (1 Thess 5:21). And why 'test'? So that you may 'retain the good' (1 Thess 5:21) and 'abstain from every form of evil' (1 Thess 5:22).

If the clouds of rain are filled, they pour out upon the earth. And this is according to the spoken truth. When things are well, when those ministered to by providence are well, that is, 'the clouds, having been filled, pour out upon the earth.' Water, if it flows into the sea, is of no use for sowing. Even if all things happening under providence are useful in some other way, they are of no use to the 'earth' if they flow into the Adriatic or into the sea. As for the literal sense, this is so; but this is for the intellect. Souls ministering to the 'word of salvation' happen to be 'clouds being filled with rain.' Moses, being a single 'cloud,' says: 'let my utterance be expected like rain' (Isa 55:10). And concerning all those who are 'raining' [being rained upon].
spiritual ascent
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Tree by the Waters and the Wind of the Spirit
english: The [good] has come, calling the south wind. And observe the cause: 'Blow through my garden and let my fragrances flow,' which the north wind does not do. And he has used more natural names; for he said 'cold wind' for the north. And the coldness closes the pores of the trees, which are called seeds, so that the parts remain inside.

But if the warm south wind blows through the garden of this soul—for the garden is according to the soul—the pores are thinned, that is, the concepts, since the fragrances are the sweet thoughts. Therefore he says this: 'Where the wood falls, there it will remain.' If the south wind blows through the soul, the fragrances flow, and where the sweet ones are, they fall.

Instead of asking, 'is there not still a transfer?', he speaks of an immediate falling, as if I say: 'All the nations will stand before the coming Savior king, to separate the goats from the sheep; and he will set the sheep on the right, but the goats from the left' (Matthew 25:32). So, 'where it fell, it remained'—the goat from the left, the sheep on the right?—Not so, if one hears the goats: 'Go into the eternal fire' (Matthew 25:41). He does not say that they will always remain there, nor does he say that those called into the kingdom will always remain there and not move into greater and super-ascended and super-cosmic places, to reach that glory which the Savior had before the world (John 17:5).

And he says this: 'Where it falls, there it will remain,' as if he says, like the one making a distinction: if it is earnest, it will remain in virtue; if it is trivial, in wickedness. And this is not doubtful, but he shows what follows; even if he spoke doubtfully, it was because of the turning of the will; but he did not speak doubtfully. Furthermore, does the 'wood' lie in another scripture? The one blessed for not having settled in the counsel of the ungodly, nor having stood...

He says that one shall not walk in the way of sinners nor sit in the seat of the ungodly, but shall be like a tree planted by the outlets of the waters. Then he brings forth a little more: 'and all that he does shall be prosperous,' showing that he speaks concerning a man; for it is not in the power of a plant to 'do' and to 'be prosperous.' And it is brought forward: 'not thus are the ungodly, not thus,' like the tree. And again in Jeremiah it is said: 'Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, whose hope is the Lord; and he shall be like a tree planted by the waters' (Jeremiah 17:7-8), and he calls it 'blessed' by the Lord. And again in the Psalms you have: 'Then all the trees of the forest shall rejoice before the face of the Lord' (Psalm 97:8).

Observing the wind, he does not sow, and seeing in the clouds, he does not reap, in which there is no knowing what is the way of the Spirit. And it is true toward the word, for when the strong 'wind' scatters the sown seed and it does not enter into the furrows of the earth as it ought. And as for an illustration, the 'wind' is often taken regarding an uncertain matter; for it has been said that 'they are carried by every wind.' If you 'observe' this 'wind,' you 'will not sow,' but when it ceases, when there is great clarity and calm; that is, just as the soul is carried about here and there by passions, it is not able to 'sow in tears' so that 'you may reap in joy' (Psalm 126:5), it is not able to 'sow into righteousness.' Therefore, 'observe' the 'wind.'

And it is possible, and indeed it is possible, for 'observing' to be used instead of 'watching closely.' The word is also taken regarding this, sometimes regarding a guard, and sometimes regarding an observation. When he says that 'the sinner will observe the righteous' and 'seeks to kill him,' he is careful, as an archer would observe, which limb of the opposing one is bare, so that he might send the arrow there. But when he says 'you will preserve us,' instead of 'you will protect us.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Way of the Spirit and the Mystery of Bone Formation
english: In the same way, the serpent cannot strike the wing of the man if it is outside the sandal. He who is 'shod with feet in preparation for the gospel' is not struck in the wing by the serpent. Thus indeed, in a manner of blessing, it is said to someone: 'iron and bronze is your sandal.' But you know that 'iron and bronze' is not received as a blessing for sandals; for it strikes the foot; for the sandal pulls the one 'shod' into its own shape and a wound occurs around the foot. Therefore, the one who has received 'authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy' (Luke 10:19) shows himself unhurt. The invincible and the unhurt are signified many times by these materials.

And seeing in the clouds, he will not reap (James 5:7). When 'he sees in the clouds,' he sees rain lying upon [the earth], 'he will not reap.' We must force the meaning of the word; if a 'rain' is lying upon [the crops], the 'rain' being driven down harms the things being reaped, making them moist, and they easily come to rot. This is therefore what the command is: in a suitable 'time' let every 'thing' be done by each one in his own way. Through these two words, he transfers them to all things.

For example, one being introduced into godliness, by way of divine knowledge, let him 'sow' when it is 'time,' receiving lessons which were fitting for the one being introduced to receive. And let him not 'reap' prematurely, but when he sees a 'rain' lying upon [the ground] capable of watering, then let him 'reap.' For at such times the harvest is taken. The diligent one begins and always has an end in the cutting ahead. The prior labors reach an end, but those following them take up the beginnings.

Such a thing, then, is this, and in the gospel the Savior says concerning the Spirit, of 'reapers' and 'sowers': 'that the sower may rejoice at the same time as the reaper' (Psalm 126:5). But it is not profitable in the same time to 'sow' and 'reap' in the sensible sense. But that of the word, the 'things being reaped' are grown, and those being grown come to 'being reaped.' For I said that some are left behind, but to others they come. For it has been said, 'when a man has completed, then he begins' (2 Timothy 4:18); and that which 'begins' and 'completes' happens 'at the same time.' The 'beginning' signifies the 'sowing,' and the 'end' the 'reaping.' 'The sower and the reaper rejoice at the same time.' And it is possible also to take it thus: when the s...

His [harvest] 'is completed', but it does not have the 'reaper'. The 'reaper', when he does not have 'seed', does not have that which 'he might reap'. Therefore, these things can happen simultaneously by the 'blessing' and 'grace of God'.

11,5a In which [ones] there is not a knowing [one], what is the way of the Spirit. He says this: that 'in which there is not a knowing the way of the Spirit', these commandments are useful. And he said that the diligent and the perfect—indeed diligent and always progressing through progresses—is both; for he knows the 'way of the Spirit'. Thus, 'is the one knowing the way of the Spirit'; 'let him watch', if it is 'wind', not 'to sow', and when 'rain' is appropriate, and not 'to reap'.

11,5bc Just as a bone in the belly of a pregnant woman [is formed], thus one will not know the 'works' of God. Regarding the incomprehensible of these 'works', it signifies either the hard-to-grasp. Those who have dealt with the nature of animals have spoken of a certain way and a sequence of change for each part; concerning 'bone' they did not have [the power] to say. 43 They say that blood is composed in such a way: when food is presented and digested—when it becomes through being sent [to be processed]—the food changes into blood; and that which is rejected must be cast out, it is not decomposed into the composition of the thing eaten, but is cast off as waste. But when it has been absorbed, then, through a change occurring successively, it is decomposed into blood. Then they say that from the blood, having become thick and congealed, flesh is made, and from the wastes of the food, hair, nails, and such things are made, which are as wastes. But concerning the generation of 'bone', none of them found [it], so that this was as 'your judgments are a great abyss' (Psalm 139:6). Such a thing is also what is said in one of the Psalms: 'My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret' (Psalm 139:15). And 'which you made in secret', he says this, that its genesis is hidden; and 'was not hidden' this [was] 'from you'. Therefore, take this for an illustration.

She 'carries' [is pregnant] the woman who has received the seed from a man. But the seed, having been cast into the womb, undergoes the first change into nature. For there is nothing other than nature or seed having thickened, having near to change into flesh. After nature, the change leads to the embryo, the embryo...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Sowing in Tears and Reaping in Joy
english: Toward the living thing, after which the manifestation immediately occurs. Just as 'it is not known' those 'in the womb of the pregnant woman,' unless by chance a revelation from God happens to occur, so the soul, which has attached itself to the seeds and the wombs of the 'bridegroom' of the Savior—about whom it is said, 'he who has the bride is the bridegroom' (Matt 9:15)—has hidden the wombs. But then they become manifest, when the wombs, which God sowed, change into thought and works. It is not therefore necessary to always have them 'in the womb.' And one has them 'in the womb' and 'bears them' who does not change the words and the thoughts of the works into works and dogmatic contemplations. Just as there 'you do not know' those things, unless they change into good works and pious contemplations, so also one 'will know the works of God' no other way than if they change into works according to energetic operation.

In order that you might receive the strong dogmas as the 'bone of the pregnant woman' by an upward leading; for the 'bones' are the sustaining things of the body. In the same way, without the dogmas of piety, the passions and the duties are not correctly placed. For this reason, it is said concerning these 'bones' that they also have 'knowledge of God' and know that no one is 'like Him.' He did not say absolutely, but rather 'in the womb of the pregnant woman'; just as if I say that when it is night nothing of the visible is seen, I am not saying that nothing is seen, but rather when it is night; for it is not the same to say 'nothing is seen' and 'at night nothing is seen.' 'In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand withhold, for you do not know which this or that will succeed' (Eccl 11:6).

Since we are very much turning toward the literal, and this is to be taken toward history. Often the name of 'day' does not signify only the illuminated air when the sun was above the earth, but also the whole life of man, as if the hymnographer says, 'and I waited for you all the day.' And often 'day' and a 'season' beginning and receiving are called the same. He says therefore that at the beginning of the 'season'—so that you might take the 'day' as one 'season' of 'sowing' and 'reaping'—he says at the beginning of that 'season,' by which there is 'sowing,' do not be slow, 'sow your seed.' For so in the 'evening' not...

Your hand finds what it will reap; when the time is fulfilled, the harvest will stand. And these things are spoken in a literal sense. But in an allegorical sense, those 'sowing in tears'—those 'sowing into the Spirit, so that they may reap eternal life'—sow in the beginning of the 'day'; and it is that 'day' which Abraham received with love and longing, so that he might 'see' and be shown by the Savior. And that 'day' is the one of which the choir of the saints says: 'This is the day which the Lord has made'. The apostle also signifies this same thing to the Romans, writing: 'the night is gone, and the day is near, as if we walk decently in the day' (Romans 13:12). Thus he says: the time of 'ignorance' is called 'night'; after this has 'passed', the 'day' succeeds it.

The beginning of the 'day' is 'morning', in which all the saints hasten. One of them says: 'I will stand before you in the morning and watch' (Psalm 118:18), and 'my God, my God, toward you I rise at dawn' (Psalm 43:3). Another says: 'out of the night my spirit rises toward you, O God' (Psalm 57:8). In this morning, 'sowing in tears', sowing the seeds of virtue with pains, sowing into the Spirit with sweat, so that you may 'reap eternal life', and having 'sown in tears you may reap in joy' (Psalm 126:5) and come 'rejoicing', bringing the sheaves of the seed. Therefore, let not 'your hand' let go of the beginning of the sowing. The word 'sow' applies to both senses.

It can also be understood thus: since, as 'walking decently in the day', they are both 'children of light' and 'children of the day', these have the 'present age' as the 'morning' of virtue, in which they owe to 'sow', so that in the 'evening' they may 'reap'. Yet that 'evening' is not theirs, but of others; for to them there will be eternal light, the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2) always touching them. You have something similar in a psalm: 'weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' (Psalm 30:5). The sun 'rises and sets' at once, but not for the same people; to those to whom it 'rises', they 'rejoice'; to those to whom it 'sets', they 'weep'. Something similar is brought in Jeremiah: 'late her voice cried out' (Jeremiah 4:19), when her 'sun' was 'setting'. And it is said in the manner of a threat: 'and the sun shall set upon the prophets'—and 'prophets' here he means...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Christ as Alpha and Omega, Beginning and End
english: The false prophets—for 'the day shall come upon them to darken them' (Eccl 11:6). Therefore, you, O man, being exhorted to 'sow in the morning, and let not your hand withhold' (Eccl 11:6) until the 'evening', so that you may receive an excellent 'harvest' of knowledge from God; for 'light your own light of knowledge, and bear fruit unto the fruit of life, until generations of righteousness come to you'.

11,6c Because you do not know what sort of thing will belong, this or that. 'You do not know', he says, 'what this or that will belong to'. If you are 'sowing' but not farming, you do not know whether it bears fruit or does not bear fruit.

328 It is also possible to take this to mean that the same person 'at once' 'sows' and 'reaps', so as not to 'belong' to one kind first and to another kind second 'at once' while all things are happening. And yesterday was a witness to the Gospel that 'so that the sower may rejoice together with the reaper' (Matt 13:43), as the same 'time' is for both 'seed' and 'harvest'; 'harvest' indeed of the progress already received, and 'seed' of the future to be received.

And the visitation of the Savior may happen to some 'in the morning' and to others 'in the evening'; 'evening' for those who were unfaithful, but 'morning' for those to whom the sun 'has risen' (Ps 118:130) through 'faith' and 'piety'. And this must be said: it is impossible to teach correctly one who has not learned.

In the very beginning of the introduction to instruction, it is 'sow and let not your hand withhold' so that one might again have a product and 'sow' and feed others. Such a blessing is brought forth in Genesis concerning Benjamin: 'Benjamin', he says, 'a wolf that snatches the morning food and will distribute food in the evening' (Gen 49:27).

The 'wolf that snatches' was when 'he persecuted the church and incited it'; [gap] ... of that state, and the rest became from 'Benjamin' the son of the right hand, the 'son of the day', the son of rest; then indeed 'he ate in the morning', being instructed in the introduction according to faith, 'and in the evening he gave food as nourishment', he became an 'apostle', a 'teacher in faith and truth among the Gentiles'.

Furthermore, what then is 'you do not know'?—since they are 'at once', you do not have the knowledge that divides this from that. To 'belong' here means to be placed together. 11,6d7ab And if the two are the same good things. And the light is sweet and good to the eyes.
To see with the sun. If, he says, 'you sow' well and 'you reap', 'the two good things have happened at once'. And you have received well the preceding progress and have received the following well.

Jesus himself therefore says to be 'beginning and end'; 'I', he says, 'am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last, the living one and I became dead, and behold, I am living forever' (Rev 1:8, 22:13). See how these things, appearing to be opposite, he says to be himself both before and after. For he says, 'I am the first and I am the last', or first, 'I am the Alpha and I am the Omega'.

There are letters which the Holy Spirit engraves in the heart of those thus prepared. For he says: 'not on stone tablets, but on fleshly tablets I engrave' (2 Cor 3:3); and he says these are written by the Holy 'Spirit', by the 'living Spirit'. He himself is also the divine letters; in which the 'book of the living' (Rev 21:27) is written, in which 'the names' of the apostles are engraved 'in the heavens' (Rev 21:27), there they are inscribed. He therefore says 'I am the Alpha and I am the Omega'.

Through other things he revealed that the other things also are. He himself is therefore 'beginning' and 'end'. It is therefore within his power to participate 'at once', in which respect he is 'beginning' and 'end'; according to one respect 'beginning', and according to another 'end'. And just as we call the same one 'lamb' and 'shepherd' and these do not conflict, so we call [him] 'way' and 'door' and these do not oppose. Thus he himself is called 'beginning' and 'end'.

'Beginning' is as a 'foundation' of the 'divine building' being laid down; 'for no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid' (1 Cor 3:11). He himself is the 'head of the corner' (Ps 118:22); he himself the 'placed foundation' 'has become the head of the corner', joining; and the 'corner' is the meeting of two walls. Just as the two covenants and the two peoples were joined and the church became one, using Christ as 'head', so also [he] became 'end'.

Behold, 'beginning and end', 'first and last'. Take the 'first' here according to honor; there are those bearing the first things 'in the church' such as 'apostles, prophets'; there are also the others having such things as 'the gift of healings, understanding, governance, tongue'. All...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Light and the Visible
english: Therefore he is that one. For they become such by imitating him. And so he is called 'first' in honor and 'last' in honor.

But if you wish to hear a deeper word: Jesus your Lord, 'passing through the heavens,' imitated all the logoi in both the ascent and the descent, just as it is carried in Isaiah to the one ascending, so that he might benefit every rank; for he did not pass through a place descending, where no benefit was accomplished. Therefore the super-ascending one can also be a living being, but the 'last' is perhaps the 'man or the one descended.' He imitated all, so that every rank might be benefited. For did not the apostle himself say, 'he has become all things to all, so that he might win all' (1 Cor 9:22)? And to those to whom 'he became all things' and who also are 'the last,' 'he became lawless to the lawless, so that he might win the lawless; a Jew to the Jews, so that he might win the Jews; wisdom to the wise' (1 Cor 9:20-22)—if then his imitator was doing these things, he does much more.

Furthermore, he says having said this: 'the living one and I was born a corpse.' 'I am the living one,' not the 'one having become living'; for he is 'living,' for he is 'life,' but 'he became' 'dead'; but the intervening part is resolved: for he came up; 'and behold, I am living forever' (Rev 1:18). For if even 'living' he happens to have 'become dead,' he has not 'become dead forever' by that 'life' shining forth, which they had before the death.

And the light is sweet and good to the eyes. In either way, the 'light is sweet' 'to the eyes and good.' It benefits the 'eyes.' And if you take it regarding the sensible, it shows him the visible things. But if regarding the divine 'light' of the eternal, about which it is said, 'was the true light, which enlightens every man' (John 1:9), 'enlightening the eyes of the heart,' it is 'sweet' to them. In either way, the 'light' and the 'eyes' must be taken, and likewise the 'sweetness.' Similarly, if he speaks about the visible things of those shown by the sensible...

The word 'sweet' is instead 'pleasant'. If you take the internal 'eyes' and the 'true light', it is 'sweet' just as it is said, 'Taste and see that the Lord is good' (Psalm 34:8) and 'Your words are sweeter than honey and wax' (Psalm 19:10), 'Eat honey, my son, for it is good wax, so that your palate may be sweetened' (Proverbs 24:13). The 'honey', that which is eaten, is the 'good', the spiritual dripping from the Scriptures; and the 'wax', in which the word of the Scriptures consists.

Regarding 11,7b, [it is] seeing with the sun. He who has this 'light' 'sees the sun'. Listen again in another way. The other visible things are shown by 'sun' and 'light'; but the 'light' itself is not shown by another, but it manifests itself. This happens both in history and in the upward ascent. To see in harmony, there must be both sight and 'light' and visible things. For there are times when, though sight exists, visible things are not perceived, when it is night. And again, when the 'light' exists, if someone does not look, even if he is not deprived of it, he does not see them. Therefore, you see these things when the 'light' ... makes them manifest for perception.

And there is something else: the 'light' that shows, the visible things that are shown, and the sight that shows. Regarding the intelligible, it is not so. The 'light' is not shown by 'light' even though it is visible, but it makes itself manifest. Moses said this, 'Show me yourself', and 'no one else is able to show me' (Exodus 33:20), just as if someone said to the 'sun', 'Show yourself to me', for no one else can show you. So also the Savior said in the Gospels: 'He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me; and he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will manifest to him' (John 14:21).

title: Memory and Eternity
english: Himself, myself. Again, 'I manifest', 'no one else shows me'. But you say that the Son 'shows the Father'. But observe that it is the essence of Father and Son; for just as the 'Father is shown' by the Son, so also the Son by the Father; 'he who has seen me', he says, 'has seen the Father' (John 14:9). And see that the Son reveals the Father, and the Father also reveals the Son. For Paul says as 'God was pleased to reveal his Son in me' (2 Cor 4:6). And Peter was testified that 'flesh and blood did not reveal' (Matt 16:17) the Son to him, but the one who begat him, the 'heavenly Father'.

11,8abcd And if a man lives many years, in them... he will be made glad and will remember the days of darkness, because many they will be. 11,8a 'Even if a man lives ten thousand years', but he was a 'man' guarding the 'image and likeness' and thus the 'man' has become as 'straight' so as to know the straightness of the light and to 'sow in the morning' and 'not to leave anything to the hand in the evening', 'he will be made glad'. 11,8ab 'Even if he lives many years, he will be made glad'. And 'many years' come from the cycle of the 'sun of righteousness' (Ps 89:11). For just as the perceptible sun, circling a certain circuit, makes 'years' and annual cycles, so also 'the true light'.

Concerning these things, therefore, the holy one who was enlightened by him says: 'I have remembered and meditated on eternal years'. If all things among us are 'temporary', how can 'eternal years' be spoken of as occurring among us? And again: 'I have remembered eternal days, understanding generations of ages'. From 'eternal days' the 'eternal years' are constructed. 'Even if a man lives many years, he will be made glad in them', if he acts thus as a 'man', if he is not 'compared alongside' and becomes 'beast-like', if he is not 'a mare of a horse', 'not wise' according to the 'half-part'.

Furthermore, the 'even if'? —since not all 'live' these 'years'; but not according to nature does the 'living one live', but if he wills, 'he lives'. If this, therefore, exists, 'he will be made glad' in all the days. Therefore, regarding the literal sense, the truth is not mentioned [as such], 'if' someone lives ten thousand 'years', '[he] will be made glad in all of them', unless you say it thus: the wise man does not rejoice only over pleasant things, but also over unpleasant things, bravely bearing them; for 'I will bless the Lord' (Ps 34:1).

"At all times," he says, even if the surrounding things were unpleasant and even if they were distressing; just as Job "at all times" "rejoiced" (Job 1:21). And he will remember the days of darkness, because they will be many (Job 20:5). Mostly, the one being in evil does not "remember" the "eternal lights", but the one being in virtue knows even the evil and "remembers" it; thus indeed he "turns away" from it. For until the present they are working, but the wicked are handed over even after these things to the darkness and to other unpleasant things, to all the punishments. The one "remembering", therefore, will not be tried by them.

However, we take "to remember" in a different way; for we also take from the use of memory many times, and the not using of forgetfulness. For when he speaks about the righteous, those enjoying the divine promises, saying "they will forget their first affliction"—instead of saying they will not be tried by it again—"nor will it fall upon their heart again". Why? "For the heaven will be new and the earth will be new"; once my cosmos has been re-measured and the promises have been fulfilled, there will no longer be memory of the distressing. And thus we have become accustomed to say: when a change occurs, we say one takes "forgetfulness of former things", whether they were good or not good. For it is said: "In a good day, the amnesty of evils" (2 Cor 4:6). For he does not say this meaning that the one tried by "days of good" and of light realized that he was being tried by "evils". But no longer does he "remember" them according to experience.

Rejoice, youth, in your youth, and let your heart make you good in the days of your youth, and walk in ways blameless and in the vision of your eyes (Eccl 11:9). "That which is coming" is not eternal; "they are temporary" regarding these "things seen", the visible creatures; but "the unseen" are also "eternal", which the saints strive to possess, saying: "Our aim is not the things seen; for the things seen are temporary, but the unseen are eternal" (2 Cor 4:18). If they are not "eternal", they are not going to be, even if perhaps "virtue" or "knowledge" were once going to be; among us this happens: if we have not become in evil or in ignorance, we are not going to have lost light or going to have goodness. Therefore by nature the divine things are outside of the "presently existing". And I remember that I have used such a sample.

title: The Nature of Evil and the Coming Good
english: At what time? The one who... [text gapped]. But it is present here, as it is about to be. And I have used such an example: that if a man, while it is day, having closed a door in a house, should block up every opening, the light is not present to him, yet it is present. If, therefore, he opens the shutters, if he casts away ignorance, he finds the light present; so that it is not 'about to be'. Therefore, everything of this kind that is 'coming' is 'vain', of the nature of the 'vain'. For 'vain' is not a reproach, unless it is through comparison with those who have risen far above. Such things were indeed said at the beginning of the book; but then we used such examples, saying that it shines and illuminates bright lights. Just as regarding the sun and the light, that which is there is the solar one; this is 'vain', not denied but inferior.

Without doubt, some wish to think regarding virtue what they also think regarding evil; for it has been said regarding evil that 'it was not from the beginning, nor shall it be unto the age' (Ps 118:160). Regarding idolatry and fornication it is indeed said, but through synecdoche, it is understood regarding all evil. And it is said that 'injustice lied about itself' (Prov 12:4). And 'to lie' is, as we say, to have 'lied' regarding the earth, as regarding grain, as regarding a vine. And some who have a shared view of the soul say that virtue is such: it does not exist without the one acting. But this is a falsehood, for it is in God, and from there we derive it. Even if we depart, the good exists in God. But the evil, if no one acts, is no longer. And regarding this, namely the primordial evil, which is called all evils after a secondary designation: for both the 'wicked' and the 'enemy' and 'death' and the 'sinner' are so called. Indeed, it is said, 'crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked' (Ps 37:24), crush his work called the 'arm'; then immediately it says: 'his sin shall be sought, and it shall not be found through itself'. 'Through itself it is not found'; for among those that exist, it is something that has happened (accidental) capable of being cast away. It is not an inseparable thing that has happened; nor does anything of the inseparable things happen, since nothing is cast away from them. In this way, nothing that happens many times remains. Furthermore, what kind of harm? It remains inseparable; except it was not always inseparable, but from the time it was established, from the time it...
the character does not change whether looking with the body

title: The Integrity of Sight and the Tripartite Soul
english: A curved road, such as those to whom the word speaks: 'O you who abandon straight paths' (Ps 15:2), whose 'paths are crooked' and 'curved.' 11,9b And let your heart make you good in the days of your youth. 'Let your heart make you good,' not the external things. It has often been said to us regarding the difference between happiness and blessedness, that some place happiness in being fulfilled by the three kinds of goods. Wealth does not 'make good,' it does not truly make one good, nor does health of the body, nor having rank and glory. But possessing virtue of the soul 'rejoices' [one]. This, therefore, is 'let your heart make you good,' not the external things, not the things concerning the body; do not think greatly upon these, and hasten not to pursue these.

11,9c And walk in blameless paths. Walk in the 'straight paths' I have spoken of clearly; for the virtues and the activities according to them and the contemplations of the truth are 'good and straight paths.' Likewise, regarding Elymas the sorcerer who perverted the human, Paul says: 'Do you not cease perverting the straight ways of the Lord?' (Acts 13:10) Not that they 'are being perverted' there, but to what extent he 'perverts' them toward that. Just as if someone presumes upon youth saying that one need not be prudent, and bears insults against prudence, for he does not make it real. Some indeed hold council with injustice; but those who hold council with such things slander justice. Therefore, 'let your heart make you good,' not the accidental things, not the bodily things. Then you will have 'blameless paths' and chance to be blessed; for 'blessed are the blameless in the way' (Ps 119:1) and 'he who walks blamelessly and works righteousness.' And see that 'walking' is not in vain; for it was possible to say both 'stand blameless' and 'sit blameless'; but the walk signifies progress. Therefore, 'walk blameless,' beginning to follow the 'way' with the 'blameless.' Such also is that which is written by Paul: 'we shall walk in newness of life' (Eph 4:24), so that we may progress 'in the newness of life.' Having stripped off the garment of the old life, 'we have put on the new man.' We have a new life, we progress in it, and not turning away from it, we shall not lack.
11,9d And in the vision of your eyes. Take it again in its entirety.

If "your heart is good," you have "eyes" that see well. And in plain words: not seeking foreign beauty, you turn the "eye" away from a prostitute; you do not see a woman for shameful desire, but you have an "unblemished" "vision of the eyes." If you also take the "enlightened eyes of the heart," called the "eyes of the reasoning," the "unblemished" state is much more established.

And know that God will judge you regarding all these things, and remove passion from your heart and drive out evil from your flesh. Do what I command you, knowing "that God will judge you in all these things." "Judgment" measures out punishments for the bad, but promises and good things for the serious. Since you do not destroy in vain, if you "walk" "unblemished in your ways" (Psalm 119:1) and "are rejoiced in the days of your youth" (Psalm 119:9), strive; for "God will bring you to judgment" regarding these. If they were bad things, for which "judgment" was made toward him, punishment was to be expected; but since they are good—for the "ways" and the divine thoughts are fitting—if you walk thus "unblemished," you do not destroy in vain; for "God leads you in these to judgment."

And remove passion from your heart. "Passion" is not a virtue of the "heart," but of the spirited part. Therefore he says: do not use your reasoning and your mind for "passion," but, even if this movement ever stands in the spirited part, restrain it in your "heart." Thus it is removed "from your heart," not by being mixed with it.

The soul is tripartite, as many have said. And the matter is such: we have various senses. Just as it is not possible to see by hearing, nor to touch or smell by intellect, so we appear to have the inner man and the soul itself. We have a spirited power, a reasoning power, and a desiring power. From where [do we know this]? Observe that the reasoning is distinct from the spirited and the desiring from the irrational animals: irrational animals have a spirited power and "passion," and a desiring power and desire, but they do not have reasoning. Since they do not have reasoning, it is evident they do not have the reasoning part, they do not have mind. And the mind is signified by the name of the "heart."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Youth and the Nature of Vice
english: He continues in the Scripture. Therefore he says that, even if you should ever be angry, do not lead the 'anger' into the 'heart', so that the 'anger' does not become a disposition. And if you should have a desire having suddenly become in the desiring part, do not carry it into the mind and the reasoning faculty; for it will be a disposition and no longer a passion or a pre-passion, but wickedness. 11,10b And lead away evil from your flesh: 'And from your flesh lead away the evil' (Eph 4:22). And unbridledness seems to be a wickedness of desire; therefore 'lead it away from your flesh'. And it is possible also thus: if 'the anger departs from your heart', you do not practice evil through the members and the body; the one being angry strikes many times and threatens and intends to murder. When therefore 'the anger departs from your heart', those things happening through actions which are evil also pass away.

11,10c.12,1abc For youth and thought are vanity; and remember your Creator in the days of your youth, until the days of your wickedness do not come (Eccl 12:1). 11,10c If the young man does not 'walk' 'in the ways blameless', nor does he do the other things which he was appointed to do, he is in 'ignorance'. It is also said in proverbs by this wise man: 'Folly spreads from the heart of a youth' (Prov 22:6). 'Ignorance' is disguised by 'youth'. If indeed anyone exceeds the movement of 'youth' and moves like an old man as if in 'youth', he has much 'ignorance'. 'That I may give cunning to the innocent, and perception and understanding to the young child'. If 'perception and understanding are given to the young child' by wisdom, it is evident that he has cast away 'ignorance'. When he does not have knowledge, he is in thoughtlessness. For this reason also in the Psalms such things were joined to 'youth': 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances' (Ps 25:7). See that 'youth' is most receptive to these things and possesses them. Therefore 'rejoice', so that you may not have 'folly'; therefore 'walk', so that you may not have 'vanity' and 'evil of the flesh'.

Regarding Ecclesiastes 12:1, therefore, in the day of your youth, remember who created you. God is the one who 'created' [Eccl 12:1]; it is not that God 'creates' vices in me. For this reason, observe that He 'created you in youth,' not so that you might have 'ignorance,' not so that you might be thoughtless, not so that you might be unlearned, but so that, being receptive to knowledge, you might take it up.

Until the days of your vice arrive [Eccl 12:1]. If he means by 'vice' this thing which is contrary to virtue and brings boastfulness to the one possessing it, he says: 'until the days of your vice do not come,' meaning as long as you are receptive to virtue and 'vice'—do not expect 'vice,' and do not prepare yourself for it. For when you possess virtue, 'vice' has no place in you. In the very young, there is the power of both, virtue and 'vice'; but in those who have surpassed the new age, such that they no longer bring the character of infants, there is no 'vice' in that soul, but only virtue. And the infant and the diligent man both flow with 'vice,' but they are different in how they are apart from 'vice.' For the diligent man, by disposition, has what is contrary to 'vice'—and this is practical virtue, the virtue of a single whole—and opposites cannot coexist; but in the infant, not having 'vice' is not a disposition, but an absence of 'vice.' If, therefore, he means 'vice' as this worst condition, 'until the days of your vice do not come,' walk 'blamelessly' [Eccl 12:1] regarding what has been commanded to you. Furthermore, does 'until they come' mean as if they are 'coming' by necessity? No, but rather as if 'vice' is being urged upon us. If I say that as long as the body of the living thing is healthy, disease does not 'come,' I am not saying it is necessary. Again, I say that as long as someone is an infant, unlearningness does not 'come' to him. I say this differently: for age hinders; it is not age that prevents disease or health, but the expression of the opposites. If, however, he means 'vice' as he means harm—for harm can be both injury and punishment—before it 'comes'...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Will of God and the Allegory of Celestial Bodies
english: Regarding punishment, the 'evil' that is coming, do what I tell you, so that the coming punitive evil may not find you liable. Does punishment come before? God brings punishment upon men not as it happens by chance, but when He judges it beneficial to bring it upon them; for the Lord is a 'righteous judge, powerful and long-suffering, not bringing wrath on every single day; if they do not turn back, He will whet His sword' (Ps 7:11). Since God is a 'righteous judge,' how is it that sinning men do not fall under punishment and retribution? Is it because, through weakness, He 'did not bring it'? No; He is 'powerful' and was able to punish immediately, but with His power He is also 'long-suffering' and 'does not bring wrath on every single day'; for those whom He 'brings wrath upon' and those whom He does not, He knows through His most profound words. Therefore, when they despise the warning of the threat because the 'evil' has been hidden, as if it were necessary only to be punished later, then 'if they do not turn back' to whom He was long-suffering, 'He will whet His sword.'

This is the 'evil' that is 'coming,' being not a habit in the hand, but a punitive, most violent affliction. In the 'time' therefore of 'judgment,' upon every 'time,' He judges all. And He calls this 'time' at once a 'time of judgment' and at once a 'day of wrath' and a 'day of retribution.' 'Until this evil comes,' 'until the evil has come,' repent. 'Repentance' has a 'place'; 'the Lord of the promise is not slow, as some think He is slow, but is long-suffering toward them, not wishing to destroy anyone, but wishing to bring all to repentance' (2 Pet 3:9). Since therefore 'repentance' is given to you as a superior thing, repent before the 'evil comes.'

And the years in which you speak will pass; I have no desire for them; until the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened and the clouds turn back the rain (Matt 24:29). If the punitive 'evil comes,' the 'years' stand in which 'you do not have' 'in them the will.' But no one wants to be punished. If the 'years' of the promises are present, the diligent have 'in them the will'; they wish to enjoy the promises by working for what brings them. For example, the lovers of good and even these sensible things...

Those who only accept [things] do not have a 'will' for a time of famine, but they have [it] for a time of prosperity. For the righteous man, then, there is a 'will' in those times when the recompenses take place. It is written in Isaiah: 'they shall desire,' says Simon, 'if the wicked have become consumed by fire' (Isa 66:24). Does not he who wills the impending wrath 'become consumed by fire'? He has his 'will' in that time.

Until the sun is darkened and the light and the moon and the stars (Matt 24:29). The time can also be taken rhetorically, and the 'years in which not' the sinner has a 'will'; it shall happen then, when 'the heaven and the earth pass away' (Matt 24:29). And 'the sun' is 'passing away' 'with the heaven and the earth,' he says, 'it shall be darkened and the moon shall not give its light' (Matt 24:29). 'Until the sun is darkened'; and it is possible to take it thus: as much as we in this life have our present existence unhindered, we are able to be illumined by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) and by the 'light of the true one' and by the 'moon and the stars.' But we take the 'moon' more allegorically as the ecclesiastical opinion; and toward the 'sun of righteousness,' 'moon' may be said to be the teaching which is able to enlighten there. And likewise, the 'stars' are taken as the ministers of the divine gift, the 'angels,' in whom God 'speaks' His 'word.' They are 'darkened,' therefore, that is, from you; for the 'sun' is by no means extinguished at once. And just as in the nights it seems to us that the 'sun' itself is 'being darkened,' not because it suffers, but because it is becoming distant from us, far from our sight, so also the 'sun of righteousness' 'is being darkened' to those who are no longer worthy of being illumined by it.

And they shall turn the clouds back behind the rain. 'Clouds' have often been said to be those ministering the spiritual 'rain,' namely men or angels. And these 'turn back' 'behind the rain,' no longer ministering the 'rain'; for it is not advantageous then for the 'rain' to come. You have an apostolic saying such as this: advise that men should be diligent, and attend to virtue and divine opinion and abstain from the opposing things; and having said this, he takes such a pattern, that regarding how much the divine teaching is, 'it is necessary to attend' and

title: Vessels of Gold, Silver, Wood, and Clay
english: bringing forth useful vegetation
It is useless to the master if it is not prepared for every good work. Thus he says: in the world there are diligent men; and these are 'vessels' of 'gold and silver' (2 Timothy 2:20).

And whoever 'purifies' their own mind and works through fire, they are 'gold vessels', having diligence concerning the intelligible things, being moved toward the supra-cosmic things. But 'silver' vessels are those ministering the word. For it has often been demonstrated that the 'word' stands for the name of 'silver'.

And I say from a clear rhetorical figure, so that this enigma may become manifest: the Spirit gives a 'word of wisdom' and a 'word of knowledge' (1 Corinthians 2:6). And you have this distinction: the one having the 'word of wisdom' and 'word of knowledge' and perceiving correctly and contemplating the scientific things and being able to speak them didactically; for they are having a 'word of knowledge', but they are not 'capable' of 'honoring'. And they truly possess precise conception and undivided knowledge, but they are not such as to carry over what has been perceived to others in a didactic manner. Thus they are having a mind having been made precise, and because of this they are 'gold vessels', but they are not such as to minister to others what has been perceived to them.

Others are 'silver', being able by word to make clear what has been perceived to them and what they read. And there are other 'vessels of wood and clay'. And of these, 'some for honor, others for dishonor' there are (2 Timothy 2:20). The 'gold and silver' are precious, but the 'wood and clay' are 'dishonorable'. The 'wood' is able to be consumed by fire, and the 'clay' is such as it is 'to be crushed'.

But natures are not introduced here as unchangeable, as the myth of the heterodox desires. For it follows that 'if anyone purifies himself from the dishonor of them', it is evident that 'as a vessel', 'he will be a vessel for honor to the master for every good work'; so that by himself someone becomes a dishonorable and ignoble 'vessel'.

There is indeed a transition occurring from the honorable to the dishonorable; for it has been said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah regarding a great change having happened to Israel from piety to impiety and from practical virtue to practical wickedness: 'the precious sons of Zion, adorned with gold' and silver, 'how they were counted as vessels of clay' (Jeremiah 9:11). You see that the precious things are made of gold and silver.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Pottery and the Rejected Vessels
english: "They were counted as shards." Likewise also the race of Israel, when it was unfaithful to the Savior, [says] "as vessels of a potter they are broken, they shall shepherd them with an iron rod" (Jeremiah 18:4); when they were sheep, they were golden and were led under a pastoral "rod", but now "with an iron rod", and "they are broken like vessels of a potter".

Immediately also in Jeremiah a mystical thing regarding such things lies; it is commanded "to go down into the fifth house of the potter, and having gone down" (Jeremiah 18:2) he saw a "vessel" being flattened, "clay" being shaped into a "vessel"; and since the dwelling did not have the form of the "vessel" of "honor", "it fell from his hands"; the potter "let it fall" so that it might be remolded by the potter. Therefore, when a place has capacity for repentance, it is a clay "vessel" capable of being remolded, of being transformed. But when it has reached a stability in a state almost unchangeable or difficult to change, then it is henceforth a "shard". For this reason it is cast away.

Furthermore, the prophet, after seeing in the "house of the potter" the shaping of the "vessel", takes a "small shard" and "breaks" it. And he says: "thus I will destroy the pride of Jacob" (Isaiah 10:22). Therefore they were rejected, therefore "they are cast out". And he says concerning this in Isaiah, of this "broken shard vessel", that thus "it was broken" (Isaiah 32:20) so that "not to be found" is a part of it "in which" anyone is able to take a little "water" or "fire", that is to say, having become completely useless, not even the "water"—the little bit or that still capable of quenching—can be received, nor the "fire" that brings to the "shard" itself hardness.

Therefore: here does he say "house" for the world or the church? For in this too there are such diverse "vessels" "for honor and for dishonor". And that such things are in the church, the divine word says: "remove the evil one from among yourselves" (1 Corinthians 5:13), "vessels of dishonor" etc. Again, "fornication is heard among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, that a man has a woman of his father" (1 Corinthians 5:1). And he commands "to cast out" this one. And the church can be the "great house" and the surrounding place. And "guards" of this "house" are those appointed to watch.
abandon
